title: Sun, Moon and stars: why the Sun is a star and the Moon is not

summary.text: The Sun is a star, the same kind of thing as the stars we see at night. It looks huge and bright only because it is so much nearer to us. Stars make their own light, while the Moon and the planets only reflect sunlight. The Earth is one of eight planets going round the Sun, and the Moon goes round the Earth. A torch carried far down a corridor shows how a huge light can look like a tiny dot.
summary.art: A night sky over an Indian rooftop: a big glowing Sun drawn in a corner with rays, a pale Moon with an arrow showing sunlight bouncing off it, a steady bright planet low in the west, and many tiny stars, each with a small faint sun-shape drawn beside it.

intro.hook: Hold up one finger at arm's length. You can hide the whole Moon behind it. But the Moon is about 3,500 kilometres wide, wider than India. How can a finger hide something so big?
intro.text: Tonight, look up from a window, a balcony or the terrace. From a city you may see only a few dozen stars, because street lights brighten the sky. Some of them twinkle. One or two bright dots may shine steadily. In the daytime the Sun is the brightest light, so bright that you must never look at it. Here is the question for this unit. Is the Sun a different kind of thing from the stars? Or is it the same kind of thing, just much closer?
intro.art: A child on a rooftop at dusk holding up one finger that hides the whole Moon, with a few stars and one steady bright dot in the sky.

outcomes: I can say what a star, a planet and a moon are, and which of them make their own light.
I can explain, using my near lamp and far lamp test, why the Sun looks big and bright but other stars look tiny.
I can tell a planet from a star in the evening sky: planets shine steadily and slowly wander among the stars.
I can describe the Sun's family: the Sun in the middle, eight planets going round it, the Earth among them, and moons going round planets.
I can explain that the Sun shines because hydrogen deep inside it joins up to make helium, and that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
I can say what scientists agree about, what they still argue about, and who did the work, including people who were not given the credit.
I can follow the idea all the way out: starlight is old light, the atoms in my body were made in stars, and many other stars have planets.
I can look at the Sun safely with a pinhole viewer, and I never look straight at the Sun.

terms.meaning: A huge ball of very hot glowing gas that makes its own light and heat.
terms.example: The Sun is a star. So is the Pole Star, Dhruva Tara.
terms.art: A glowing ball of gas with flames of light at its edge, and a tiny dot version of it beside it labelled 'the same thing, far away'.

terms.meaning: The star at the middle of our solar system. It is the nearest star to us, so it looks big and bright.
terms.example: The Sun lights and warms the Earth every day.
terms.art: The Sun drawn huge, with a tiny Earth beside it to show their sizes.

terms.meaning: A big round world that goes round a star. A planet makes no light of its own. It shines because starlight bounces off it.
terms.example: The Earth, Mars and Jupiter are planets. They all go round the Sun.
terms.art: A round planet with sunlight arrows hitting one side and bouncing off.

terms.meaning: A smaller world that goes round a planet. Our Moon goes round the Earth about once a month. It shines only with sunlight that bounces off it.
terms.example: Jupiter has many moons. The Earth has one, which we call the Moon.
terms.art: The Earth with the Moon going round it on a dotted path.

terms.meaning: An object that goes round a planet. The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. People also send up satellites made of metal.
terms.example: Weather satellites go round the Earth and photograph the clouds.
terms.art: The Earth with the Moon and a small metal satellite both going round it.

terms.meaning: The path one thing follows as it goes round and round another.
terms.example: The Earth's orbit round the Sun takes one year.
terms.art: A dotted oval path round the Sun with the Earth on it.

terms.meaning: To bounce light back. Things we see that make no light of their own are reflecting light.
terms.example: A steel plate shines in torchlight because it reflects the light.
terms.art: A torch beam hitting a steel plate and bouncing off towards an eye.

terms.meaning: Something that makes its own light. A thing that makes its own light is called luminous.
terms.example: The Sun, a candle flame, a firefly and a torch are light sources.
terms.art: A row of glowing things: the Sun, a candle, a firefly, a torch.

terms.meaning: Makes no light of its own. We see a non-luminous thing only because light falls on it and it reflects some of that light into our eyes.
terms.example: The Moon, the planets, your face and a mirror are non-luminous.
terms.art: A row of lit-up things with arrows showing light arriving and bouncing off: the Moon, a planet, a mirror, a face.

terms.meaning: The Sun and everything that goes round it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets like Pluto, rocks called asteroids, and icy comets.
terms.example: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun in our solar system.
terms.art: The Sun with eight planets on their orbits and a few moons and comets.

terms.meaning: To flicker. A star twinkles because our moving air bends its tiny point of light this way and that.
terms.example: Stars low in the sky twinkle most. Planets usually shine steadily.
terms.art: A twinkling star seen through wavy lines of air above a rooftop.

terms.meaning: The old name for a planet. The word planet comes from a Greek word meaning wanderer, because planets slowly move among the stars.
terms.example: Over a few weeks, Venus moves past the stars around it.
terms.art: A bright planet dot moving along a dotted trail past fixed stars, night by night.

terms.meaning: A pattern of stars that people have joined up and named. The stars in it may be very far apart.
terms.example: The Saptarishi, seven bright stars shaped like a ladle, is part of a constellation.
terms.art: The seven stars of the Saptarishi joined by thin lines into a ladle shape.

terms.meaning: The distance light travels in one year. Light is the fastest thing there is, so a light-year is a giant distance.
terms.example: The nearest star after the Sun is about 4 light-years away. Its light takes about 4 years to reach us.
terms.art: A beam of light racing across a long ruler marked with a calendar at the end.

terms.meaning: A giant group of billions of stars, held together by gravity. Our galaxy is called the Milky Way, or Akash Ganga.
terms.example: Far from city lights, on a dark night, you can see part of the Milky Way as a faint white band. From a city you cannot.
terms.art: A spiral galaxy with a tiny arrow on one arm saying 'our Sun is here'.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see.
terms.example: Your body, the Sun and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a child's hand to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: The two simplest, lightest kinds of atom. Stars are made mostly of them.
terms.example: The Sun is about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium. Helium is the gas in floating balloons.
terms.art: A cut-open Sun shown as a jar of mostly hydrogen balls and some helium balls.

terms.meaning: When the centres of tiny atoms are squeezed so hard that they join together. Joining gives out a huge amount of energy. This is what makes stars shine.
terms.example: Deep inside the Sun, hydrogen joins up to make helium. The energy comes out as sunlight.
terms.art: Four small hydrogen balls being squeezed together into one helium ball with a flash of light.

terms.meaning: A card with a tiny hole that lets sunlight through to make a small picture of the Sun on paper. It is a safe way to look at the Sun.
terms.example: Stand with your back to the Sun. The round spot on the paper is a picture of the Sun.
terms.art: A child with their back to the Sun holding a card with a pinhole, and a small bright circle on a white sheet.

terms.meaning: A planet going round a star other than our Sun.
terms.example: Scientists have found more than 6,000 exoplanets.
terms.art: A faraway star with a small planet beside it, and our tiny Sun shown far away in the corner.

terms.meaning: A tube with lenses or mirrors that gathers lots of light, so faint and faraway things look brighter and bigger.
terms.example: With a small telescope you can see craters on the Moon and the rings of Saturn.
terms.art: A child looking through a small telescope at the Moon, a grown-up beside them.

explanations.concept: Light sources and reflected light: stars, planets and moons
explanations.definition: A star makes its own light. A planet is a big round world that goes round a star. A moon goes round a planet. Planets and moons make no light. We see them because sunlight bounces off them.
explanations.description: Everything we see either makes its own light or reflects light that falls on it. The Sun, a candle and a firefly are light sources. Your face, a steel plate and the Moon make no light. They only reflect it. In a completely dark room you cannot see your own hand, because there is no light for it to reflect. The night sky works the same way. Every star is a light source. The Moon and the planets reflect the Sun's light.
examples: The Moon looks bright at night, but it is only reflecting sunlight, like a steel plate in torchlight.
Venus, the brightest dot in the evening sky, is a planet lit by the Sun. It makes no light.
About 1,500 years ago, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the Moon and the planets are lit by the Sun, with one half bright and one half dark.
explanations.art: Two columns: light-makers (the Sun, a star, a candle, a firefly) and light-bouncers (the Moon, a planet, a steel plate, a face), with arrows showing light coming from the Sun to the bouncers.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: some lights in the sky make their own light, and some only reflect it.

explanations.concept: The Sun is a star, the nearest one
explanations.definition: The Sun is a star. It is the same kind of thing as the stars we see at night. It looks so much bigger and brighter only because it is so much nearer to us.
explanations.description: The Sun is enormous. About 109 Earths would fit across its middle, side by side, like beads on a string. More than a million Earths could fit inside it. It is about 15 crore kilometres away. That is 150 million kilometres. A car going at 100 kilometres an hour, day and night without stopping, would take about 170 years to get there. Its surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, far hotter than any kitchen fire. The next nearest stars are about 270,000 times further away than the Sun. That is why they look like pinpricks.
examples: If the Earth were a peppercorn, the Sun would be a ball about as big as a football, 24 metres away.
A torch held near your face looks big and dazzling. The same torch far down the road looks like a small dot.
From a planet round a faraway star, our Sun would look like one more small star in the sky.
explanations.art: A football-sized Sun and a peppercorn Earth on a long path, with a measuring tape between them.
explanations.context: Is the Sun a different thing from the stars? This card answers the puzzle from the start of the unit.

explanations.definition: The further away a light is, the smaller and dimmer it looks. It looks smaller because it takes up less of what you see. It looks dimmer because its light spreads out on the long trip, so less of it reaches your eye.
explanations.description: Think of a lamp in a dark room. Close up, a lot of its light goes into your eye, so it looks bright. Far away, the same light has spread out over a much bigger space, so only a little of it reaches you. Stars are so far away that even a giant sun becomes a faint dot. Distances to stars are so big that we measure them by how long their light takes to reach us. Light travels about 3 lakh kilometres every second. That is fast enough to go round the Earth more than 7 times in one second. Even so, light from the nearest star after the Sun takes about 4 years to get here.
examples: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Moonlight takes just over 1 second.
Light from Sirius, the brightest star at night, takes about 8 and a half years to reach us.
So when you look at a star, you see it as it was when its light set off, long ago.
explanations.art: A torch beam spreading out like a cone, with a big bright splash close to the torch and a faint thin patch far away.
explanations.context: Remember the near lamp and far lamp test, where a torch looked smaller and dimmer as it moved away? This card explains why, and what it means for stars.

explanations.concept: Why stars twinkle and planets mostly don't
explanations.definition: Stars twinkle because our moving air bends and shakes their light on its way to our eyes. Planets look like tiny round discs, not points, so they usually shine steadily.
explanations.description: Out in space, starlight is steady. The twinkle is made here, in our own air. Air is always moving, with warm and cool patches, and each patch bends light a little. A star is so far away that it reaches us as one tiny point of light. The moving air shakes that point about, so it flickers. A planet is much nearer, so it reaches us as a very small disc. The air shakes each part of the disc differently, and the wobbles even out. So a planet looks steady. Near the horizon, where we look through the most air, even planets can twinkle a little.
examples: Astronauts above the air see stars shining with no twinkle at all.
A bright, steady dot in the west soon after sunset is very often Venus or Jupiter.
Stars near the horizon twinkle more than stars high overhead, because their light passes through more air.
explanations.art: Two beams coming down through wavy layers of air: a thin one from a star, zig-zagging, and a thicker one from a planet, staying steady.
explanations.context: This card explains a trick for telling a planet from a star: watch whether it twinkles.

explanations.definition: Night after night, the stars keep the same patterns. Planets slowly move against those patterns. The word planet comes from an old Greek word that means wanderer.
explanations.description: The whole sky seems to turn each night, because the Earth spins. But the stars keep their places in their patterns, year after year. A few bright dots do not. Over days and weeks, they drift past the stars. People in India, Greece, China and Babylon noticed these wanderers thousands of years ago. You can see five of them without a telescope: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. They move because they are going round the Sun, as the Earth is. In old Indian astronomy, these five, with the Sun and the Moon, were counted among the nine grahas. Today we sort them differently: the Sun is a star, the Moon is a moon, and the five are planets.
examples: Venus is called the morning star or the evening star, but it is a planet. In India it is called Shukra.
Mars, Mangal, shines with a red-orange colour because its ground is covered in rusty dust.
Planets always stay close to one narrow path across the sky, the same path the Sun and the Moon follow.
explanations.art: Five nights of the same star pattern drawn side by side, with one bright dot moving a little further along each night.
explanations.context: This card explains a second way to find a planet: it moves among the stars over many nights.

explanations.concept: The Moon: the Earth's companion with borrowed light
explanations.definition: The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. It goes round the Earth about once a month. It makes no light. Moonlight is sunlight that has bounced off the Moon.
explanations.description: The Moon is about 3 lakh 84 thousand kilometres away. It is about a quarter as wide as the Earth. The Moon is not white. Its ground is dark grey. It reflects only about 12 out of every 100 parts of the sunlight that hit it, about as much as an old tar road. It looks bright only because the night sky around it is so dark. The Moon always keeps the same face towards us, because it spins round once for each trip round the Earth. Its other side is not dark. It gets just as much sunlight. We simply never see it from Earth. Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it goes round us, we see more or less of that lit half, so it seems to change shape.
examples: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. They found grey dust and rocks.
On 23 August 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole, the first spacecraft to land there.
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and also about 400 times further away. That is why they look about the same size in our sky.
explanations.art: The Moon half lit by sunlight arrows, with a patch of its grey dusty ground shown next to a strip of old tar road for comparison.
explanations.context: This card is about the brightest light in the night sky, the Moon, and where its light really comes from.

explanations.definition: The Sun sits in the middle of our solar system. Eight planets go round it, and the Earth is one of them. Gravity is the force that pulls things towards each other. The Sun's gravity keeps the planets going round it.
explanations.description: In order from the Sun, the eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The first four are small and rocky. The next four are giants made mostly of gas and ice. The Sun is far bigger than all of them put together. Of all the matter in the solar system, about 998 parts out of every 1,000 are in the Sun. Each planet keeps moving forwards, and the Sun's gravity keeps bending its path into a loop. The Moon goes round the Earth in the same way, held by the Earth's gravity. The Earth goes round the Sun once a year, carrying the Moon with it.
examples: Jupiter is the biggest planet. About 1,300 Earths would fit inside it, but it is still tiny next to the Sun.
Pluto used to be called the ninth planet. In 2006 astronomers voted to call it a dwarf planet.
There is far more empty space in the solar system than anything else.
explanations.art: The Sun with eight planets on their orbits, the Earth highlighted with its Moon, and a faint dotted line from the Sun to each planet to show gravity.
explanations.context: This card is about the Sun's family: the planets that go round it, with the Earth among them.

explanations.definition: The Sun shines because of nuclear fusion. Deep in its middle, hydrogen atoms are squeezed together so hard that they join to make helium. Joining gives out a huge amount of energy, which comes out as light and heat.
explanations.description: The middle of the Sun is about 15 million degrees Celsius, and the Sun's own weight squeezes it tighter than anything on Earth. There, the centres of hydrogen atoms crash and join. Every second, the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of its own matter into energy. That is like the weight of hundreds of thousands of elephants, gone into light every second. It has been shining for about 4 and a half billion years. It has enough hydrogen to keep going for about 5 billion more. People once thought the Sun was a giant fire. But a Sun made of burning coal would have burnt out in a few thousand years. In 1920 Arthur Eddington, an English astronomer, suggested the Sun runs on hydrogen turning into helium. In 1939 Hans Bethe, a German-American physicist, worked out exactly how.
examples: Every second, trillions of tiny particles from the Sun, called neutrinos, pass straight through your body. They even pass through the whole Earth at night.
The energy made in the Sun's middle takes many thousands of years to work its way out to the surface. After that, it reaches us in 8 minutes.
Scientists in India and around the world are trying to build fusion machines to make clean electricity, the way the Sun does.
explanations.art: A cut-open Sun with a glowing core where small hydrogen balls join into helium balls, and arrows of light working their way out to the surface.
explanations.context: The Sun has been shining for billions of years. This card explains what keeps it going.

explanations.concept: What stars are made of, and who found out
explanations.definition: Stars, including the Sun, are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Scientists found this by splitting starlight into its colours and reading the dark lines in it.
explanations.description: Shine sunlight through a prism and you get a rainbow. Look very closely and the rainbow has thin dark lines in it. Each kind of atom makes its own set of lines, like a fingerprint. So starlight tells us what a star is made of, without anyone going there. But the lines are hard to read, because heat changes them. In 1920 Meghnad Saha, a scientist from a poor family in a village near Dhaka, worked out how a star's heat changes its lines. In 1925 Cecilia Payne, a young English student at Harvard in the United States, used Saha's idea on the lines of many stars. She found that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, not the same mix as the Earth. The most famous astronomer in America at the time, Henry Norris Russell, told her this was impossible. She softened her claim. Four years later, Russell agreed with her, and for years many books gave him the credit.
examples: The Sun is about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium. All the other kinds of atom together make only about 2 parts in every 100.
Helium was first found in sunlight, in 1868, before anyone found it on Earth. Its name comes from Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.
Meghnad Saha was nominated for a Nobel Prize several times but never won it.
explanations.art: Starlight going through a prism into a rainbow with thin dark lines, a young woman at a desk of glass photo plates, and a young Indian man writing equations.
explanations.context: How can we know what a star is made of, when nobody can ever go there? This card tells how, and who worked it out.

explanations.concept: Star colours tell how hot they are
explanations.definition: Stars come in colours. Blue-white stars are the hottest. Yellow-white stars like the Sun are in the middle. Orange-red stars are the coolest.
explanations.description: A blacksmith's iron glows dull red when it is hot, then orange, then yellow-white when it is even hotter. Stars work the same way. Even from a city you can see that some bright stars are orange and some are blue-white. Annie Jump Cannon, who worked at Harvard in the United States, sorted about 350,000 stars by their light, more than anyone else in history. She was almost completely deaf. Her system, with the letters O, B, A, F, G, K and M from hottest to coolest, is still used by every astronomer. The Sun is a G star. The Sun is really white. It looks yellow from the ground because our air scatters away some of its blue light.
examples: On winter evenings, from December to March, find Orion in the east or high in the south. Betelgeuse at one shoulder is orange-red. Rigel at the opposite foot is blue-white. Both are bright enough to see from a city.
Betelgeuse, called Ardra in India, is so big that if it sat where the Sun is, it would swallow Mars's orbit.
From space, astronauts see the Sun as a brilliant white.
explanations.art: A row of stars from blue-white to yellow-white to orange-red, with a glowing iron rod beside them going from red to white.
explanations.context: Look closely at the brightest stars and you will see different colours. This card explains what their colours mean.

explanations.concept: Stars are born and die, and the atoms in us were made in stars
explanations.definition: Stars are born from huge clouds of gas and dust, shine for millions or billions of years, and then die. Inside them, and when they die, new kinds of atoms are made. Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star.
explanations.description: When a star like the Sun runs low on hydrogen, it starts joining helium into carbon and oxygen. Big stars go further and make heavier atoms, up to iron. When a big star dies, it blows up in a huge explosion called a supernova, and scatters these atoms into space. New stars, planets and living things form from those scattered atoms. In 1957, four scientists, Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle, showed how stars make the atoms. Margaret Burbidge was the expert who measured the starlight. Only Fowler later got a Nobel Prize for this work. The Sun will not explode. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a huge red star, then shrink into a small, hot, dim star called a white dwarf.
examples: The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born.
The hydrogen in the water you drink is older still. It was made at the very start of the universe.
Scientists think much of the gold on Earth was made when two dead stars crashed together. They watched one such crash in 2017.
explanations.art: A star exploding and scattering glowing dust, which drifts into a new solar system, and finally into a child holding a glass of milk and a spinach leaf.
explanations.context: Stars are not forever. This card follows a star from birth to death, and finds out what that has to do with you.

explanations.definition: Many stars have planets going round them. A planet going round another star is called an exoplanet. Scientists have found more than 6,000 of them.
explanations.description: For hundreds of years, people wondered if other suns had planets. In 1584 an Italian thinker, Giordano Bruno, wrote that the stars are suns with worlds of their own. The church of his time put him on trial for his beliefs, and in 1600 he was put to death. Nobody could check, because a planet near a star is far too faint to see next to its sun. In 1992 two astronomers, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail, found the first planets round another star, a strange dead star called a pulsar. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, in Switzerland, found the first planet round a star like the Sun. They noticed the star wobbling a tiny bit as its planet tugged on it. Today we know there are probably more planets than stars in our galaxy.
examples: Some exoplanets go round their star in just a few days, much closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
Some stars have several planets, like a small solar system of their own.
Nobody knows yet whether anything lives on any exoplanet.
explanations.art: A faraway star wobbling slightly as a planet goes round it, with a scientist's graph line going up and down beside it.
explanations.context: If the stars are suns, do they have planets too? This card is about the answer, found only about 30 years ago.

explanations.description: The Moon has been with the Earth for about 4 and a half billion years. How it got there is still argued about. Moon rocks brought back by astronauts are very like the rock deep inside the Earth. Any good idea has to explain that.
examples: Astronauts brought back about 382 kilograms of Moon rock and dust between 1969 and 1972.
The Moon has only a tiny iron centre, while the Earth has a big one.

perspectives.who: Most scientists today, following William Hartmann and Donald Davis, two American scientists, in 1975
perspectives.explanation: When the Earth was very young, a planet about the size of Mars crashed into it. The crash threw out a huge cloud of hot rock, which came together to make the Moon. Scientists call this the giant impact idea.

perspectives.who: Some scientists today, including Simon Lock and Sarah Stewart, in 2018
perspectives.explanation: The crash may have been so big that the young Earth became a spinning doughnut of hot vapour. The Moon formed inside that cloud. This could explain why Moon rocks and Earth rocks are so alike.

perspectives.who: Older ideas, now mostly given up
perspectives.explanation: George Darwin, the son of Charles Darwin, suggested in 1879 that a fast-spinning Earth flung the Moon off. Others thought the Earth caught a passing Moon. Neither idea fits what we now know about Moon rocks.

explanations.art: A young glowing Earth being hit by a smaller planet, with a ring of hot rock spreading out that slowly gathers into a Moon.
explanations.context: The Moon has always been there for every human who ever lived. This card asks how it got there, a question scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: What we can see is only a small part
explanations.description: Stars and the glowing gas around them are what we can see. But in the 1970s Vera Rubin, an American astronomer, and her colleague Kent Ford measured how fast stars go round in galaxies. The outer stars were moving far too fast. With only the matter we can see, their galaxies should fly apart. Something unseen seems to be holding them. When Vera Rubin was a student, Princeton University would not let her study astronomy there, because it did not take women. She kept working, and never got a Nobel Prize.
examples: If dark matter is real, there is about five times as much of it as all the stars, planets and gas put together.
Huge machines deep underground are waiting to catch a single particle of dark matter. None has been caught yet.

perspectives.explanation: There is unseen matter, called dark matter, that pulls with gravity but gives no light. Nobody knows yet what it is made of.

perspectives.who: Mordehai Milgrom, an Israeli physicist, in 1983, and some others
perspectives.explanation: Maybe there is no hidden matter. Maybe gravity works a little differently over the huge distances of a galaxy. This is a minority view, but it is still being tested.

explanations.art: A spiral galaxy drawn in bright dots, wrapped in a much bigger faint dotted cloud labelled 'unseen?'.
explanations.context: We have been learning about the lights we can see. This card is about a surprise: what we see may be only a small part of what is there.

agreed.text: The Sun is a star, the same kind of thing as the stars we see at night.
agreed.evidence: Split the Sun's light and a star's light into colours, and both have the same kinds of dark lines, made by the same atoms. In 1838, Friedrich Bessel measured how far away a star was for the first time. It was so far that it had to be as bright as a sun to be seen at all.

agreed.text: Stars make their own light. The Moon and the planets shine only with reflected sunlight.
agreed.evidence: The Moon changes shape as we see more or less of its sunlit half. In 1610 Galileo saw through his telescope that Venus changes shape in the same way. Spacecraft that visited the planets found rock, gas and ice, not fire.

agreed.text: The Earth and the other planets go round the Sun.
agreed.evidence: Galileo saw four moons going round Jupiter, so not everything goes round the Earth. Over a year, nearby stars seem to shift a tiny bit, as the Earth moves round its orbit. Spacecraft fly to the planets using a map with the Sun in the middle, and they arrive.

agreed.text: The Sun shines by nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen into helium.
agreed.evidence: Fusion makes tiny particles called neutrinos. Since the 1960s, detectors deep underground have caught neutrinos from the Sun. At first they caught only about a third of the number fusion predicts. In 2001 a detector in Canada showed that the missing ones had changed type on the way. Counted together, the numbers match.
Since 1992, astronomers have found more than 6,000 planets round other stars. Some are seen as a tiny dip in their star's light when the planet passes in front.

agreed.text: Bright lights at night hide the stars from most people.
agreed.evidence: In 2016, scientists led by Fabio Falchi made a world map of night-sky brightness. They found that more than a third of all people can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live.

chart.title: Of every 100 people in the world, how many can see the Milky Way from home (an estimate from 2016)

data.label: Cannot see it: about 36 out of 100
Can still see it: about 64 out of 100

challenging.claim: Stars are small sparks or little holes in a dark sky-cloth, much smaller than the Moon.
challenging.who: Many people in the past. Children everywhere still think this at first.
challenging.for: Stars look tiny. They are much smaller than the Moon to our eyes.
challenging.against: Things look smaller the further away they are. When astronomers measured how far away stars are, they found that stars must be as bright as suns to be seen at all. Many are much bigger than the Sun.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of what stars are, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: The Sun and everything else in the sky go round the Earth.
challenging.who: Ptolemy, a Greek astronomer in Egypt, about 1,850 years ago, and most people for the next 1,400 years
challenging.for: That is what it looks like. Every day the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, and we do not feel the Earth moving.
challenging.against: In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus showed the planets make more sense going round the Sun. In 1610, Galileo saw moons going round Jupiter. Today spacecraft fly round the solar system using the Sun-centred map. Long before, in 499 CE, Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins, which is why the stars seem to turn.
challenging.context: This card is about the biggest change in how people pictured the sky.

challenging.claim: The Sun is a giant fire, burning like coal or wood.
challenging.who: Many people in the past, and most children today
challenging.for: The Sun is hot and bright, like a fire. Fire is the hottest thing most of us have seen.
challenging.against: A Sun made of coal would have burnt out in a few thousand years. The Earth is about 4 and a half billion years old. Fire also needs oxygen from the air, and space has none. The Sun shines by fusion, not by burning.
challenging.context: The Sun looks like a huge fire. This card asks whether it really is one.

challenging.claim: The Sun is just an average, ordinary star.
challenging.for: There are billions of stars like it in our galaxy. It is not the biggest or the hottest. Its type, a G star, is a common one.
challenging.against: Most stars, about three out of four, are small, dim red stars called red dwarfs. The Sun is brighter than about 9 out of every 10 stars in our galaxy. So it is ordinary in kind, but bigger and brighter than most.
challenging.context: This card asks whether our Sun is an ordinary star or an unusual one. The answer depends on what you compare it with.

challenging.claim: The Moon makes its own light.
challenging.who: Many people long ago, and many young children
challenging.for: The Moon glows brightly at night, like a lamp in the sky.
challenging.against: Anaxagoras in Greece, about 2,450 years ago, and Aryabhata in India, in 499 CE, both said the Moon shines with the Sun's light. The Moon's changing shape shows it: we see only the part that faces the Sun. Moon rock brought back by astronauts is dark grey, and it gives off no light.
challenging.context: The Moon is the brightest light in our night sky. This card asks where that light comes from.

challenging.who: Most drawings and most of us
challenging.for: The Sun looks yellow, and orange or red when it is low at sunrise and sunset.
challenging.against: Astronauts in space see the Sun as brilliant white. Our air scatters some of the Sun's blue light across the sky. That is why the sky is blue and the Sun looks a little yellow from the ground.
challenging.context: Everyone draws the Sun yellow. This card asks what colour it really is.

challenging.claim: Henry Norris Russell discovered that stars are made mostly of hydrogen.
challenging.for: Russell published this in 1929. He was the most famous astronomer in America, so people trusted his name.
challenging.against: Cecilia Payne showed it in 1925, in her student thesis. Russell had told her it was impossible, so she wrote that her result was probably not real. Her work rested on an idea from Meghnad Saha in India. Today most astronomers give the credit to Payne.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for finding out what stars are made of.

big_questions.q: If the Sun is a star, and every star is a sun, could someone on a faraway planet be looking at our Sun right now, and calling it just a star?
big_questions.hint: What would the Sun look like from very, very far away? Think of the torch at the end of the road.

big_questions.q: When you look at a star, you see light that left it years ago. Are you seeing the star now, or the star as it used to be?
big_questions.hint: Light from some stars set off before your grandparents were born. Could a star have changed since then?

big_questions.q: Moonlight is really sunlight, bounced off the Moon. Is anything you see really its own light?
big_questions.hint: Your face, a leaf and a book make no light of their own. What lights them up?

big_questions.q: Is the Sun 'ours'? Or is it just the star we happen to live near?
big_questions.hint: Plants, animals and people on Earth all live on its light. Does that make it ours, or do we belong to it?

big_questions.q: The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars. Are those atoms really yours, or are you borrowing them for a while?
big_questions.hint: Where was the iron in your blood before it was in you?

big_questions.q: Why did people in India, Greece and China all count the Sun and the Moon with the wandering planets? Were they wrong, or just sorting things in a different way?
big_questions.hint: How would you sort the lights in the sky if you only had your eyes?

big_questions.q: Cecilia Payne's measurements said one thing, and a famous astronomer said another. How can a scientist find out which one is right?
big_questions.hint: Could someone else repeat her measurements on other stars? What would they find?

big_questions.q: The Sun will not shine for ever. In about 5 billion years it will swell up, then fade. Is anything in the universe forever?
big_questions.hint: The atoms a star makes go on to make new stars, planets and living things.

big_questions.q: Most of what holds galaxies together may be something we cannot see at all. How can we study something we cannot see?
big_questions.hint: You cannot see the wind, but you can see the trees move.

big_questions.q: Bright city lights hide the stars from more than a third of all people. Who should decide how dark our nights should be?
big_questions.hint: Think of birds, baby turtles, moths, sleeping people and stargazers.

big_questions.q: Is there anyone out there, on a planet round another sun? If there is, what might they wonder about?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have found more than 6,000 planets round other stars. Nobody knows yet if anything lives on them.

story.title: The Lamp That Looked Like a Star
story.note: Sai, Karthik, Mrs Fernandes, the lighthouse and the night at sea are made up. Real lighthouses do flash in their own patterns, so sailors can tell them apart, and their lights can be seen from about 30 kilometres away or more.
text: Sai was nine, and she had been inside the lighthouse. That made her different from her cousin Karthik, who was eleven and knew everything. The lighthouse stood on the black rocks at the end of the bay, striped red and white. One hot afternoon in May, the keeper, Mrs Fernandes, let her climb all one hundred and twelve steps to the top.

At the top was the lamp. Sai had expected something like the lantern in their kitchen. Instead there was a giant glass beehive, taller than her father, made of rings and rings of thick, curved glass. In the middle sat a bulb as fat as a coconut. 'The glass gathers the light into a beam,' said Mrs Fernandes. 'The whole thing turns. The boats see two quick flashes, then darkness, then two flashes again. Every lighthouse on this coast has its own pattern, so the sailors know which one they are looking at.'
'Can the boats see it from very far?' Sai asked.

'Thirty kilometres and more,' she said. Then she tapped the great glass. 'But from out there, it does not look like this. From out there, my lamp looks like one small star sitting on the edge of the sea.'
Sai did not believe her. Nothing that big could ever look that small.

That evening on the roof, Karthik explained the sky to her. 'The Sun is the king,' he said. 'It is the biggest fire there is. The stars are its little sparks. They are tiny, like the sparks from Amma's wood stove.' Sai looked up. The stars did look like sparks. But she remembered the beehive of glass, and she said nothing.

In the last week before the monsoon, the sea was flat and the fish came close. Sai's father let both children come out on the boat for one night, to help with the nets. Her aunt came too. They left at dusk with a lantern swinging at the front. Behind them, the lighthouse began to wink. Two flashes and darkness. Two flashes and darkness. It grew smaller and smaller as the land slid away.

They fished until the sky was thick with stars. Sai hauled at the net until her arms ached, and silver mackerel jumped and slapped in the bottom of the boat. Her hands smelled of salt. She was so busy that she did not notice the haze creeping out from the shore, low and grey, while the sky above stayed clear.
Then the engine coughed, and stopped.

The sudden quiet was enormous. Her father and her aunt bent over the engine with a torch, muttering. The boat rocked and turned slowly in the current. By the time the engine spluttered back to life, nobody could say which way they were facing. The haze had swallowed the coast. There were no village lights, no lights of the road. There was only black water all around, and stars.
'Look for the lighthouse,' said her father. 'Everyone look.'
Karthik stood up and stared hard into the dark, turning all the way round. 'It's gone,' he said, and his voice went high and thin. 'The haze has eaten it. If it was there, we'd see it. It's huge.'
Sai stared too. She was looking for something huge, something like the glass beehive. There was nothing like that anywhere. Her stomach went cold.
Then she heard Mrs Fernandes in her head. From out there, my lamp looks like one small star.

Sai stopped looking for something big. She looked low, along the very edge of the sea, where the stars came down to meet the water. There were dozens of little lights there. Most of them shivered and twinkled in the thick air near the water. She looked at each one in turn, slowly, counting. One star. Another star. Then one tiny light, no brighter than the others, went out. It came back twice, quick, quick, and went dark again.
Two flashes, then darkness.
'There,' she said. 'That one. It's not a star. It's our lamp.'
Her father looked where she was pointing. He waited, counting under his breath. Two flashes. Darkness. Two flashes. He let out a long breath and turned the boat towards it.

All the way home, the little star grew. It became a bright point, then a glare, then a turning beam that swept over their heads. When they came round the rocks into the bay, the lighthouse towered above them, as big as it had always been. It had never been small at all.
The next night, Sai and Karthik lay on the roof again. Karthik was quiet for a long time. 'How did you know?' he said at last.
'Mrs Fernandes said her lamp would look like a star,' said Sai. 'And it did. A lamp taller than Appa, and it looked like a star.'

She looked up at the sky, at all those tiny sparks. A new thought came to her, so big that it made her sit up. If the lamp looked like a star from thirty kilometres, what would a whole Sun look like, from very, very far away?

Karthik opened his mouth to say something about sparks. Then he closed it again. The two of them lay still and looked at the stars, and the stars looked like stars. But Sai could not stop wondering. Somewhere out there, was there another girl in another boat on another dark sea, looking at our Sun, and thinking it was only a small star?
story.epiphany: For the parent: the lighthouse lamp is huge, yet from far out at sea it looks like a small star. Karthik cannot find it because he is looking for something big. Sai finds it because she understands that distance makes huge lights look tiny. That is the key to this whole unit. The stars are not small sparks. They are suns, so far away that they look like points. And our own Sun, seen from far enough away, would be just one more small star.
ask: Why couldn't Karthik find the lighthouse, even though it was there all along?
How did Sai tell the lighthouse apart from the stars low over the sea?
Karthik said the stars are tiny sparks. What would Sai say to him now?
At the end, Sai wonders about a girl on another planet looking at our Sun. What do you think that girl would see?
Mrs Fernandes told Sai something she did not believe at first. Have you ever learned something true that seemed impossible?

games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 24 sky and home cards to cut out
items: Sirius, the brightest star at night
A cat's eyes shining in the dark
The Earth, seen from the Moon
A road sign shining in car headlights
The space station, a bright dot moving across the sky

printables.title: Two playing mats
items: LIGHT SOURCE: makes its own light
REFLECTOR: shines only by reflecting light from something else

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: does this thing make its own light, or does it only reflect light? Put it on the LIGHT SOURCE mat or the REFLECTOR mat.
Then say where the light comes from. For a reflector, say what lights it up. A good reason wins one star token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together, now or tonight. The first to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most star tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two mats on the floor, LIGHT SOURCE on one side and REFLECTOR on the other. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down in a pile. 3. Put the star tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Some things make their own light. We call them light sources. Other things only reflect, or bounce back, light that falls on them. For each card, we decide which it is, and where its light comes from.
flow.kid: Put the two mats down: LIGHT SOURCE and REFLECTOR. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, decide. Does it make light, or reflect it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the game Light Source or Reflector. It is a card game about which things make their own light and which only reflect it. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'The Moon'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'The Moon.' It looks bright at night. Is it a light source or a reflector?
flow.kid: Practice card: the Moon. Is it a light source or a reflector? Tap your answer.

ask.q: If the Moon is a reflector, what is lighting it up?
good: The Sun.
Sunlight reflects off the Moon to us.

check.q: The Moon. Light source or reflector?
options: LIGHT SOURCE: it makes its own light
check.why: The Moon makes no light. Sunlight hits it and reflects off to our eyes. That is why we only see the part of it that faces the Sun. Picking LIGHT SOURCE is very common, because the Moon looks like a lamp in the dark sky. It looks bright only because the sky around it is so dark.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it and puts it on a mat. 2. They say where its light comes from. 3. Give one star token for each good reason.
flow.say: When you put your card down, tell me where its light comes from. If it's a reflector, what is lighting it up?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on LIGHT SOURCE or REFLECTOR. Say where the light comes from. Good reasons win a ⭐.
flow.parent: Light sources: the Sun, Sirius, the Pole Star, a firefly, a candle, lightning, a lighthouse lamp, a shooting star and a phone screen. A shooting star is a speck of space dust glowing hot as it rushes into our air. Reflectors: the Moon, Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn's rings, a steel plate, your face, cat's eyes, the Earth seen from the Moon, a road sign and the space station. The space station shines only with sunlight, which is why you see it soon after sunset or before sunrise, when it is sunny up there but dark down here.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first. Save the sky tests for tonight.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess what will happen. Then let's try it and see who was right.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! First, guess what will happen. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: With the torch off in a dark room, why can't we see the steel spoon?
good: There is no light for it to reflect.
The spoon makes no light of its own.

flow.think: A mirror can look very bright. But does it ever shine in a completely dark room?

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Look at the two piles together.
flow.say: Look at the LIGHT SOURCE pile. How many of those are in the sky? Look at the REFLECTOR pile. What lights almost all of them up?
flow.kid: Count your stars. Who won? Now look at the REFLECTOR pile. What lights most of them up?
flow.think: Almost everything you see is lit by something else. What lights you up?

games.context: This is a card game about light in the sky and at home. Players decide whether each thing makes its own light (a light source) or only reflects light from something else (a reflector).

games.title: Spot the Wanderer

printables.title: A night-sky board: black paper with 25 star dots and one dotted path across it
items: 25 white star dots in fixed places, including the seven stars of the Saptarishi
One dotted path across the middle, marked 'the path of the Sun, Moon and planets'

printables.title: Wanderer tokens (beads, or small circles of coloured paper)
Sky-watcher's log
items: Did I spot it? Yes or no

rules: Put the wanderer tokens on the dotted path, each next to a different star.
The sky-watcher looks at the board for 20 seconds, then closes their eyes. This is one night passing.
Another player moves ONE wanderer a little way along the dotted path. The Moon may move a big step. Planets move only a small step.
The sky-watcher opens their eyes and points at the wanderer that moved. One point if right.
Take turns being the sky-watcher. After 5 rounds each, the highest score wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the night-sky board on a table. 2. Put the three planet beads and the paper Moon on the dotted path, each next to a different star.
flow.say: Thousands of years ago, people with no telescopes watched the sky every night. They noticed that a few bright dots moved among the stars. They called them wanderers. Let's see if you can spot a wanderer too.
flow.kid: Put the beads and the paper Moon on the dotted path. Each one goes next to a star. These are the wanderers.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spot the Wanderer. It is a memory game about how people first noticed that planets move among the fixed stars.

flow.do: 1. The sky-watcher studies the board for 20 seconds, then closes their eyes. 2. Another player moves one wanderer along the path. 3. The sky-watcher opens their eyes and points. 4. Swap roles each round.
flow.say: Remember where everything is. Close your eyes. A night is passing. Now open them. Which wanderer moved?
flow.kid: Look hard for 20 seconds. Close your eyes. Now open them. Which wanderer moved? Point to it!

ask.q: How did you know which one moved?
good: It was next to a different star.
The stars stayed in the same places, but it didn't.

flow.parent: In the real sky, the Moon moves the most. It shifts about its own width every hour, so by the next evening it has moved a long way. Venus and Mars move a little each night. Jupiter and Saturn move very slowly, over weeks. All of them stay close to the same path across the sky.

flow.do: Talk together about why the planets move and the stars do not.
flow.say: The stars are so far away that they seem fixed in their patterns. The planets are our neighbours, going round the Sun like the Earth. As we all move, they seem to drift past the faraway stars.
flow.kid: Stars are very far away, so they seem fixed. Planets are our neighbours. They go round the Sun, like us. So they seem to wander.

check.q: Why do planets seem to wander among the stars?
options: They are much nearer than the stars, and they go round the Sun like the Earth
The stars are moving and the planets are still
check.why: Planets are our neighbours, going round the Sun. As they and the Earth move, they seem to drift past the far-off stars. The stars move too, but they are so far away that their patterns hardly change in a whole human life. Picking 'the stars are moving' mixes up which is near and which is far.

flow.think: The stars do move, but so slowly that our eyes can't see it. What patterns would people see in a million years?

games.context: This is a memory game. One player secretly moves a planet bead a little among paper stars, and the other must spot which one moved, just as ancient sky-watchers spotted the planets.
