items.p: Sort these. Does each one make its own light, or shine with reflected light?
items.a: see items
items.why: Stars, including the Sun, and fireflies make light. The Moon, planets like Jupiter and a steel plate only reflect light that falls on them.

items.p: What is the Sun?
items.why: The Sun is a star, the nearest one to us. Picking 'a fire of burning coal' is a sensible guess, because it is hot and bright. But a coal Sun would have burnt out long ago. The Sun shines by fusion, atoms joining together.

items.p: The Moon goes round the ____.
items.why: The Moon is the Earth's satellite. It goes round the Earth about once a month.

items.p: Stars are tiny sparks, much smaller than the Moon.
items.why: False. Stars are suns, and many are bigger than our Sun. They look tiny only because they are so far away.

items.p: In the near lamp, far lamp test, what happened to the torch as it moved far away?
items.why: The torch did not change at all. Its light spread out over the long distance, so less reached your eye. Picking 'it went out' usually means the far dot was so faint it was hard to see. Look carefully: it is still there, just small.
items.context: In the near lamp, far lamp test, a helper holds a torch and walks slowly away from you in a dark place.

items.p: In the near lamp, far lamp test, your helper walked 40 steps away. Predict what the torch would look like at 100 steps. What does this tell you about a star that looks like a faint dot?
items.context: In the near lamp, far lamp test, a helper holds a torch and walks slowly away from you in a dark place.
items.a: At 100 steps the torch would look even smaller and fainter, maybe just a tiny dot. But it would still be the same torch. So a star that looks like a faint dot could be a huge, bright sun that is very far away.
items.why: A strong answer predicts smaller and dimmer, says the torch itself did not change, and carries the idea over to stars: how small a light looks depends on how far away it is, not only on how big it is.

items.p: Why does the Sun look so much bigger than other stars?
opts: It is the biggest star in the universe
It is much nearer to us
The other stars are switched off in the day
items.why: The Sun is our nearest star. Other stars are hundreds of thousands of times further away. Picking 'the biggest star' is a common guess. In fact many stars are far bigger than the Sun.

items.p: Match each thing to what it is.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The Sun is a star, the Earth is a planet going round it, the Moon goes round the Earth, and the Saptarishi is a pattern people see in the stars.

items.p: Soon after sunset, you see a very bright dot in the west. It shines steadily and does not twinkle. What is it most likely to be?
items.why: Planets usually shine steadily, while stars twinkle. A bright steady dot in the west after sunset is very often Venus. Picking 'a star' is natural, because people call Venus the evening star. But it is a planet.

items.p: The word planet comes from an old Greek word that means ____.
items.why: Planets slowly wander among the stars from night to night, so people long ago called them wanderers.

items.p: Divya says, 'The Moon is a small star, because it shines at night.' Use what you saw in the Own Light or Reflected Light test to explain her mistake.
items.context: In the Own Light or Reflected Light test, you put a steel plate, a white ball and a torch on a table, make the room dark, and see which things you can still see.
items.a: In the dark, the steel plate and the ball vanished, but the torch did not. The plate and the ball only shone when the torch lit them. The Moon is like the ball: it only shines because sunlight falls on it. A star makes its own light, like the torch.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test as evidence: things that make light can be seen in the dark, things that reflect light cannot. Shining at night does not make something a star. What matters is where its light comes from.

items.p: Why can't we see stars in the daytime?
opts: They go away in the day
The sunlit sky is too bright
items.why: The stars are still there in the day, shining as always. Sunlight lights up our air, which drowns out their faint light. Picking 'stars only shine at night' is very common. Stars shine all the time. We just cannot see them against the bright sky.

items.p: Put these in order, from NEAREST to us to FURTHEST: the Sun, the Moon, the Andromeda galaxy, the nearest star after the Sun.
items: the nearest star after the Sun
items.a: order shown
items.why: Light from the Moon takes about 1 second to reach us. From the Sun, about 8 minutes. From the nearest other star, about 4 years. From the Andromeda galaxy, about 2 and a half million years.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. Draw arrows to show where the Moon's light comes from and where it goes.
items.a: An arrow from the Sun to the Moon, and another arrow from the Moon to the Earth.
items.why: Moonlight starts at the Sun, bounces off the Moon and then reaches our eyes on Earth.
items.art: A blank space with a small label 'Sun' on the left.

items.p: Never look straight at the Sun. Write how you can look at the Sun safely.
items.a: Stand with my back to the Sun. Let sunlight go through a tiny pinhole in a card. Look at the small bright circle it makes on white paper. That circle is a picture of the Sun.
items.why: A pinhole viewer lets you see a picture of the Sun without looking at the Sun itself. Looking at the Sun, even for a short time or through sunglasses, can hurt your eyes for ever.
items.context: In the pinhole Sun experiment, you make a tiny hole in foil on a card and let sunlight shine through it onto white paper.

items.p: Look at the chart. A helper walked away with a torch. Each time, Meera, aged 9, gave the torch a brightness score from 5 (dazzling) to 1 (just a faint dot). At which distance did the torch look dimmest?
items.why: At 40 steps the torch scored 1, the lowest. It was the same torch every time. Only the distance changed. Picking 2 steps usually means the chart was read upside down. A taller bar here means brighter, not dimmer.
items.context: In the near lamp, far lamp test, a helper holds a torch and walks away from you in a dark place. You give it a brightness score each time.

chart.title: How bright the torch looked (made-up results)
chart.y: Brightness score (5 is dazzling, 1 is a faint dot)

items.p: The Sun is about 109 times as wide as the Earth. In the kitchen model, the Earth is a peppercorn. How big should the Sun be?
opts: About the size of a football
About the size of a lemon
items.why: A peppercorn is about 2 millimetres wide. 109 peppercorns in a row make about 22 centimetres, about as wide as a football. Picking a lemon is a common guess, because the Sun looks small in the sky. But a lemon is only about 30 peppercorns wide.
items.context: In the kitchen-table model, you make the Sun, the Earth and the Moon at the right sizes using a peppercorn for the Earth.

items.p: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. If the Sun suddenly stopped shining, we would keep seeing it for about ____ minutes.
items.why: The light that already left the Sun would still be on its way to us. It takes about 8 minutes to cross the 15 crore kilometres, so we would see the Sun for about 8 more minutes. A strong answer explains that we always see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago.

items.p: Through the night, the stars slowly move across the sky in circles. One star, the Pole Star, called Dhruva Tara, hardly moves at all. Why?
opts: It is almost straight above the Earth's North Pole, the point the Earth spins round
It is the nearest star to us
It is the brightest star, so it is held still
It is fixed to the sky, and the other stars are not
items.why: The stars do not really circle. The Earth spins, so the whole sky seems to turn. A star in line with the Earth's spin seems to stay still, like the middle of a spinning plate. Picking 'the brightest' is a common guess, but many stars are brighter than the Pole Star.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one go round the Sun, or round a planet?
items.a: see items
items.why: Planets go round the Sun. Moons go round planets. Of course, moons travel round the Sun too, carried along with their planet.

items.p: Stars low down near the horizon twinkle much more than stars high overhead. Twinkling is caused by moving air bending starlight. Explain why stars near the horizon twinkle more.
items.a: Light from a star low down passes through much more air to reach me than light from a star overhead. More air means more moving warm and cool patches to bend the light, so it twinkles more.
items.why: A strong answer uses the cause of twinkling, moving air, and adds the key fact: a star near the horizon is seen through a much thicker slice of air. This is also why astronauts above the air see no twinkling at all.

items.p: A planet low down near the horizon can twinkle a little too.
items.why: True. Planets look like tiny discs, not points, so they usually shine steadily. But low near the horizon their light passes through so much moving air that they can twinkle a little. So steady light is a good clue for a planet, not a perfect rule.

items.p: What makes the Sun shine?
opts: Hydrogen joining up to make helium, deep inside it
items.why: Deep in the Sun, hydrogen atoms are squeezed so hard they join into helium, and that gives out huge energy. This is called fusion. Picking 'reflecting light from other stars' mixes the Sun up with the Moon, which only reflects light. The Sun is a light source.

items.p: Stars are made mostly of hydrogen and ____.
items.why: Cecilia Payne found this in 1925 by reading the lines in starlight. The Sun is about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium.

items.p: Pluto was called the ninth planet for 76 years. In 2006, astronomers voted to call Pluto a dwarf planet instead. People still argue about it.

views.says: A planet must be round, go round the Sun, and have cleared its path of other big objects. Pluto shares its path with many icy bodies, so Pluto is a dwarf planet.

views.who: Alan Stern, the scientist who led the spacecraft that flew past Pluto
views.says: Pluto is round, has five moons, mountains of ice and a thin sky of air. It does everything a planet does. It is a planet.
If Pluto counts, then Eris and other icy bodies just as big must count too. We could end up with dozens of planets.

items.ask: Do you think Pluto should be called a planet? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer takes a side with a clear reason. For example, against: the rule of clearing the path keeps the list short and clear, and Ananya is right that Eris is about as big as Pluto. Or for: Pluto is round, has moons and weather, like the planets. It then admits a fair point from another side.
items.why: This is a real argument about how to sort things, not about facts. Everyone agrees on what Pluto is like. They disagree about where to draw the line for the word 'planet'.

items.p: Match each star colour to how hot that star is.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Like a blacksmith's iron, which glows red, then orange, then white as it gets hotter, a star's colour shows its heat.

items.p: Venus is the brightest dot in the evening sky, after the Moon. Why is it so bright?
opts: It is near to us, and covered in white clouds that reflect lots of sunlight
items.why: Venus comes closer to us than any other planet, and its thick white clouds reflect most of the sunlight that hits them. Picking 'it is a star' is natural, because it is called the evening star. But Venus is a planet. It makes no light of its own.

items.p: In the pinhole Sun experiment, what is the small bright circle on the white paper?
opts: A picture of the Sun, made by sunlight through the tiny hole
Just a hole in the paper
items.why: Light from every part of the Sun passes through the pinhole and lands on the paper, making a small round picture of the Sun. If a cloud passes, you see it cross the circle. Picking 'a shadow' is a common idea. But a shadow is dark, and this circle is bright.
items.context: In the pinhole Sun experiment, you stand with your back to the Sun and let sunlight through a tiny hole in foil onto white paper.

items.p: Karthik says stars are tiny sparks. Use the lighthouse lamp from the story to explain why they might be giant suns.
items.a: The lighthouse lamp was taller than Sai's father. But from far out at sea it looked like a small star. So a light can be huge and still look tiny if it is very far away. The stars could be giant suns, very, very far away.
items.why: A strong answer uses the story as evidence: the lamp was huge, yet looked like a small star from far out at sea. It then links looking small to being far away, not to being small.
items.context: In this unit's story, a lighthouse lamp taller than a man looks like one small star from a fishing boat far out at sea.

items.p: The Moon's ground is as dark grey as an old tar road. So why does the Moon look so bright at night?
items.a: The Moon is in strong sunlight, and the sky around it is black. Even a dark grey thing looks bright when sunlight falls on it and everything around it is darker.
items.why: Brightness depends on what is around a thing. A grey road in sunshine looks bright next to a dark tunnel.

items.p: Draw the Sun with three planets going round it. Then draw one moon going round one of the planets. Label each one.
items.a: The Sun in the middle, three planets on round paths around it, and a small moon on a small path round one planet, all labelled.
items.why: Planets go round the Sun. Moons go round planets.
items.art: A blank page with a small circle labelled 'Sun' in the middle.

worksheets.title: Atoms from Stars and Big Ideas (challenge)

items.p: The Sun and the Moon look about the same size in our sky because they really are about the same size.
items.why: False. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times further away. The two cancel out, so they look the same size. That is why the Moon can just cover the Sun in a total eclipse.

items.p: The iron in your blood was made inside stars.
items.why: True. Iron is made inside stars. When some of those stars exploded, long before the Sun was born, they scattered it into space. Some of it ended up in the Earth, in food and in you.

items.p: In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found the first planet going round a star like the Sun. They never saw the planet. They saw the star wobble a tiny bit, back and forth. How could a planet you cannot see make its star wobble?
items.a: The planet and the star pull on each other with gravity. As the planet goes round, it tugs the star a little towards it, first one way and then the other. So the star wobbles in time with the planet going round.
items.why: A strong answer uses gravity working both ways: the star pulls the planet, and the planet pulls the star. The wobble repeats every time the planet goes round. Mayor and Queloz won a Nobel Prize for this in 2019.

items.p: A ____ is the distance light travels in one year.
items.why: A light-year is a distance, not a time, even though it has 'year' in its name.

items.p: A star is 500 light-years away. When did the light you see tonight leave it?
opts: It never left. The star is right here
items.why: A light-year is how far light goes in a year. So light from 500 light-years away has been travelling for about 500 years. Picking 'tonight' is very natural, because the starlight seems to arrive instantly. But even light needs time to cross such a distance.

items.p: Why can't the Sun be a giant fire of burning coal?
opts: A coal Sun would have burnt out in a few thousand years, but the Earth is billions of years old
Coal is too heavy to float in space
Coal burns blue, and the Sun is white
There is no reason, it could be coal
items.why: Even a Sun-sized ball of coal would burn out in a few thousand years. Fire also needs oxygen from air, and space has none. Picking 'too heavy to float' is a common idea. But the Sun does not need to float. Its own gravity holds it together. The Sun shines by fusion.

items.p: Put these in order of size, SMALLEST first: the Earth, the Sun, the Moon, Betelgeuse (a giant red star), Jupiter.
items.a: order shown
items.why: The Moon is about a quarter as wide as the Earth. Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth. The Sun is about 109 times as wide. Betelgeuse is hundreds of times as wide as the Sun.

items.p: In old Indian astronomy, the Sun and the Moon were counted among the nine grahas, along with five planets. How do scientists sort them today?
opts: The Sun is a star, the Moon is a moon, and the five are planets
The Sun and the Moon are both planets
items.why: Ancient sky-watchers grouped together everything that moved against the stars. Today we sort by what things are: the Sun makes its own light, the Moon goes round the Earth, and the planets go round the Sun. Picking 'all seven are planets' follows the old grouping. That grouping was about how they move, not what they are.
items.context: Long ago, sky-watchers in India grouped together the lights that move against the fixed stars. They called them grahas.

items.p: How do scientists know what stars are made of, without ever going there?
opts: They split starlight into colours and read the dark lines in it
Space rocks bring pieces of stars to Earth
items.why: Each kind of atom leaves its own pattern of lines in starlight, like a fingerprint. Picking 'astronauts have visited stars' is a common idea. No person or spacecraft has ever reached another star. The nearest would take tens of thousands of years with today's rockets.

items.p: Is our Sun an ordinary star, or a special one? Give one reason for each side. Then say what you think.
items.a: A strong answer gives a reason for each side, then decides. Ordinary: there are billions of stars like it, and it is not the biggest or hottest. Special: it is brighter than about 9 out of 10 stars, and it is the only star we know with life near it.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What makes an answer strong is a real reason on each side and a clear choice at the end.

items.p: Imagine one day with no Sun at all. Write three things that would change, and say why.
items.a: For example: it would be dark, because there would be no light to bounce off things. It would get very cold, because the Sun warms the Earth. Plants could not make food, so animals and people would go hungry. The Moon would vanish too, because it shines only with sunlight.
items.why: A good answer links each change to light or heat from the Sun. Noticing that the Moon would disappear shows real understanding.

items.p: Vera Rubin found that stars at the edges of galaxies move too fast. With only the matter we can see, the galaxies should fly apart. What might this tell us?
items.a: Maybe there is extra matter we cannot see, called dark matter, whose gravity holds the stars in. Or maybe gravity works a bit differently over huge distances. Scientists are still testing both ideas.
items.why: A good answer gives at least one idea and says that it is not yet known for sure.
items.context: Vera Rubin was an American astronomer who, in the 1970s, measured how fast stars go round in galaxies.

items.p: Bright streetlights help people at night, but they also light up the sky. On Chennai's beaches, baby sea turtles hatch at night and should crawl towards the sea.

views.who: Selvi, an auto driver in Chennai
views.says: Bright lights keep the roads safe. I need to see people walking and dogs crossing. Do not make the streets darker.

views.who: Meenakshi, who helps sea turtles on the beach
views.says: Baby turtles crawl towards the brightest light. Near bright streetlights, they crawl the wrong way, onto the road, instead of to the sea.
Most children in our city have never seen the Milky Way. The light shining up into the sky is wasted, and it hides the stars.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give a reason from this unit. Then suggest one idea that could help more than one of them.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example that light shining up into the sky helps no one on the road. It then looks for a fix that helps more than one person, like lamps that shine only downwards, dimmer orange lights near the beach in the hatching months, or lights that switch off late at night.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Light keeps people safe, but light that goes up or sideways hides the stars and confuses turtles and birds. Lamps that point down give drivers the light they need, with much less glow in the sky.

items.p: Moonlight falls on your face. When did that light leave the Sun?
opts: It did not come from the Sun. It was made on the Moon
At the very start of the universe
items.why: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Moon, and just over 1 more second to reflect down to you. Picking 'made on the Moon' means the Moon is still being thought of as a light source. It only reflects the Sun's light.
items.context: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth and the Moon. Light from the Moon takes just over 1 second to reach us.

items.p: Sirius looks like the brightest star in our night sky. Betelgeuse is a giant red star that gives out thousands of times more light than Sirius. Use the near lamp, far lamp test to explain why Sirius still looks brighter to us.
items.context: In the near lamp, far lamp test, a helper holds a torch and walks slowly away from you in a dark place.
items.a: Sirius is much nearer to us than Betelgeuse. In the test, the same torch looked dimmer the further away it went. Betelgeuse is so much further away that most of its light spreads out before it reaches us, so it looks dimmer than Sirius.
items.why: A strong answer separates how much light a star gives out from how bright it looks. Sirius is about 9 light-years away. Betelgeuse is hundreds of light-years away. Distance wins.

items.p: Imagine you lived on a planet going round a very faraway star. What would our Sun look like from there?
opts: One small point of light, a star
You could not see it at all, because the Sun only shines on Earth
items.why: From very far away, our Sun would look like one more star in the sky. Picking 'only shines on Earth' is a common idea. But the Sun sends light out in every direction, across the whole galaxy.

experiments.title: Near Lamp, Far Lamp: why do stars look so small?
experiments.question: Does a light look smaller and dimmer when it is further away, even if the light itself does not change?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When the helper walks far away with the torch, will it look the same, smaller, or bigger? Brighter, or dimmer? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same torch every time, held at the same height and pointing the same way, at the watcher's chest. Change only one thing: how far away it is. Give it a score at each distance, so you can compare.
results_table: How big it looked (as big as a coin, a pea, a grain of rice or a dot)
Brightness score (5 is dazzling, 1 is a faint dot)

materials.item: a torch, or a phone with its torch switched on
the longest dim space you have: a building corridor, the terrace at dusk, or two rooms in a line with the lights off
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up is the helper. Never shine a torch straight into someone's eyes from close up. Point it at the chest.

schedule.what: Guess. Watch the torch at 2, 10, 20 and 40 steps. Score how big and bright it looks. Then talk about stars.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each distance. Then draw a bar chart of the brightness scores, one bar for each distance.

flow.do: 1. Go to the longest dim space you have. A building corridor with its lights off, the terrace at dusk, or two rooms in a line all work. 2. Ask your child to guess what will happen as the torch moves away.
flow.say: I'm going to walk away with this torch. The torch won't change at all. Do you think it will look the same as I walk away, or different?
flow.kid: A grown-up will walk away with a torch. Guess first. Will it look the same, smaller or bigger? Brighter or dimmer?

good: Far things look smaller.
Cars far down the road look tiny.

flow.context: This is the first step of the near lamp, far lamp test. You watch one torch as it moves further and further away.

flow.do: 1. Stand 2 big steps away, holding the torch at chest height, pointing at your child's chest. 2. Your child scores its size and brightness. 3. Walk to 10 steps, then 20, then 40, pointing the torch towards them each time. 4. At each stop, your child writes the scores in the table.
flow.say: Look at the torch. How big does it look? As big as a coin, a pea, a grain of rice, or a dot? And how bright, from 5 for dazzling to 1 for just a faint dot?
flow.kid: Look at the torch. How big does it look? How bright? Give it a score from 5 to 1. Write it down. Do it again at each stop.
flow.parent: Keep the torch pointing the same way each time, so the test is fair. At 40 steps it should look like a small faint point, a lot like a star. If your space is shorter, use 2, 5, 10 and 15 steps instead. The darker the space, the more the far torch looks like a star.

flow.do: Walk back to your child. Hold the torch next to them so they can see it has not changed.
flow.say: Look, it's exactly the same torch. It didn't shrink. So why did it look so tiny?
flow.kid: Look at the torch up close. Did it shrink? No! So why did it look tiny far away?

check.q: The torch looked tiny and dim far away. Why?
options: It was far away, so its light spread out and less reached my eyes
check.why: Nothing about the torch changed. Its light spread out over the long distance, so only a little reached your eyes. Picking 'the batteries ran out' is a sensible guess. But when it came back, it was just as bright as before. Distance alone made it look small and dim.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below and wait for your child's answer. 2. Then talk about the stars and the Sun.
flow.say: The Sun is a star, like the stars at night. It is the nearest one, so it looks big and bright. The other stars are suns too, so far away that they look like the torch at 40 steps, only much, much further.
flow.kid: The Sun is a star. It is our nearest one. Other stars are suns too. They are just very, very far away.
flow.think: If you could fly far, far away from the Sun, what would it look like?

ask.q: The stars look like tiny dots, just like the far torch. What might they really be?
good: Big lights that are very far away.
Maybe they are suns, very far away.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: far-away lights look smaller and dimmer, so stars could be big suns. What I saw: at 2 steps the torch was dazzling, a 5, but at 40 steps it was a tiny dot, a 1. Why: the light spreads out over the distance, so less of it reaches my eyes.

experiments.context: This is the near lamp, far lamp test. A helper walks away from you with a torch. You watch it get smaller and dimmer, and find out why the stars look so tiny.

experiments.title: Own Light or Reflected Light? A Moon in your room
experiments.question: Which things make their own light, and which only shine when light falls on them?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In a completely dark room, which of these will you still be able to see: a steel plate, a mirror, a white ball, a phone screen that is on, a lit candle? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Test every object in the same dark room. First look at each one with the torch off. Then shine the same torch on each from the same distance, about one big step.
results_table: Can I see it with the torch off?
Does it shine with the torch on?

materials.item: a torch, or a phone torch
a steel plate, a small mirror, a white ball or an orange, and a second phone with its screen on, if you have one
a candle in a holder, lit by a grown-up (optional)
a room you can make dark

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up lights the candle. Keep it in a steady holder, away from curtains and hair.

schedule.what: Test each object in the dark, with the torch off and then on. Then make a Moon with a ball and the torch.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the ball with its bright side towards the torch.

flow.do: 1. Put the objects on a table. 2. Make the room as dark as you can. 3. Wait a minute for your eyes to get used to the dark. 4. Ask which objects you can still see.
flow.say: Now it's dark. Which of these can you still see? Which have vanished?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Wait a minute. Which things can you still see? Which have vanished?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Own Light or Reflected Light test. You find out which things make their own light by looking at them in the dark.
flow.parent: Close the curtains and switch off every light, including the hall. In a city flat a little light from street lamps may still creep in. Then the plate and the ball will be faint, not gone. That faint shine is reflected street light, which is part of the answer.

flow.do: 1. Switch the torch on. 2. Shine it on each object in turn, from about one big step away. 3. Fill in the table together.
flow.say: Now let's give them light. Which ones shine now? Where is their light really coming from?
flow.kid: Switch on the torch. Shine it on each thing. Which ones shine now? Where does their light come from?

ask.q: The steel plate shines brightly now. Is it making light?
good: No, it's reflecting the torch's light.
It was invisible in the dark.

flow.do: 1. Hold the torch still, shining across the room. 2. Your child holds the white ball at arm's length and turns slowly round on the spot, watching the ball.
flow.say: This ball is the Moon. The torch is the Sun. Your head is the Earth. Turn slowly and watch the ball. Which side of it is bright?
flow.kid: The ball is the Moon. The torch is the Sun. You are the Earth. Hold the ball out. Turn slowly. Which side is bright?

check.q: Which side of the ball is always bright?
check.why: The ball makes no light, so only the side the torch shines on is bright. The real Moon is the same: the half facing the Sun is always lit. Picking 'the side facing me' is very common. We see the whole lit half only when the Sun is behind us, so its light falls on the side we see.

flow.think: If the real Moon is like this ball, why does it seem to change shape during the month?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Moon only reflects light, like the steel plate. What I saw: in the dark, the plate and the ball vanished, but the phone screen and candle stayed bright. With the torch on, only the side of the ball facing the torch was bright. Why: they make no light, so they only shine when light falls on them.

experiments.context: In this test you find out which things make their own light and which only reflect it, using a dark room and a torch. Then you use a ball as a model Moon.

experiments.title: The Pinhole Sun: see the Sun without looking at it
experiments.question: Can a tiny hole make a picture of the Sun? Does the picture get bigger if the paper is further from the hole?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the spot of light on the paper be square like the card, round like the Sun, or the shape of the hole? What will happen to its size when you move the paper further away? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same pinhole every time. Change only one thing: how far the paper is from the hole. Measure the spot at 50 centimetres, 1 metre and 2 metres.

materials.item: a piece of stiff card with a hole about the size of a coin cut in the middle
a square of aluminium foil, taped over the hole, with a pinhole poked in it
a sheet of white paper, or a white wall in shade
a ruler and a measuring tape (a tailor's tape works)

experiments.safety: NEVER look at the Sun, and never look through the pinhole at the Sun. Not with sunglasses, and not for a second. Stand with your back to the Sun and look only at the paper. A grown-up stays with the child for the whole experiment.

schedule.what: At a time when sunshine comes onto your balcony, terrace or through a window, make the pinhole card. Catch the Sun's picture on paper at three distances. Measure it.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the bright spot at each distance, at its real size.

flow.do: 1. Cut a hole about the size of a coin in the middle of the card. 2. Tape the foil over the hole. 3. Poke one small, neat hole in the foil with a pin.
flow.say: Today we will see the Sun without ever looking at it. Never look at the Sun itself. It can hurt your eyes for ever, even with sunglasses on.
flow.kid: Never look at the Sun. Not even for a second. Today you will see the Sun's picture on paper instead.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pinhole Sun experiment. You make a card with a tiny hole that will make a safe picture of the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Find direct sunshine: a balcony, the terrace, or a sunny window with the glass open. 2. Stand with your back to the Sun. 3. Hold the card up so its shadow falls on the white paper, on the floor or on a wall. 4. Find the small bright spot in the middle of the card's shadow. 5. Hold the card 1 metre from the paper and measure the spot.
flow.say: Look only at the paper, never up. See the bright spot in the card's shadow? That little circle is a picture of the Sun.
flow.kid: Back to the Sun! Look only at the paper. Find the bright spot in the shadow. That spot is the Sun's picture.

ask.q: The hole is a tiny rough dot. Why is the bright spot round?
good: Because the Sun is round.
It's a picture of the Sun, not of the hole.

flow.parent: At 1 metre the spot is about 1 centimetre wide. It should be round even if the hole is a bit ragged, because it is a picture of the round Sun. A smaller, neater hole gives a sharper but dimmer picture. If your flat gets no direct sun, do this on the terrace or downstairs, with a grown-up.

flow.do: 1. Move the card to 50 centimetres from the paper and measure the spot. 2. Then try 2 metres. A grown-up stands on the floor and holds the card high, while the child measures. The spot must land inside the card's shadow, or it is too faint to see.
flow.say: Let's see what happens when the paper is further from the hole. Measure the spot each time.
flow.kid: Move the card closer, then further away. Measure the spot each time. What happens?

check.q: When the paper was further from the pinhole, the Sun's picture was…
check.why: The light from the Sun spreads out after it goes through the hole, so the further the paper, the bigger the picture. At 1 metre it is about 1 centimetre wide, and at 2 metres about 2 centimetres. The same light is spread over a bigger circle, so it looks dimmer. Picking 'smaller' usually comes from thinking further means smaller, as with the torch. Here the hole is making a picture, and the picture grows.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a pinhole makes a small picture of the Sun. What I saw: the spot was round even though the hole was rough. It was about 1 centimetre wide at 1 metre and 2 centimetres at 2 metres. Why: light from every part of the Sun goes through the hole and lands on the paper, and it spreads out more the further it goes. Here is a bonus fact. The Sun is about 108 of its own widths away from us. That is why the picture is about 1 centimetre wide for every 108 centimetres of distance.

experiments.context: In this experiment you make a tiny hole in foil and use it to catch a picture of the Sun on white paper. It is a safe way to see the Sun, because you never look at the Sun itself.

activities.title: Everything in the Sky: a sorting game

materials.item: about 15 small slips of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, even when you are naming it.

schedule.what: List everything you have ever seen in the sky. Sort the list two ways.

activities.record: Keep the sorted slips. Stick them in two columns on a page and give each column a title.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to name everything they have ever seen in the sky, day or night. 2. Write each thing on a slip of paper.
flow.say: Let's make a list of everything you have ever seen up in the sky, in the day or at night. Anything at all.
flow.kid: Name everything you have ever seen in the sky. Day or night. Write each one on a slip of paper.
flow.parent: Good lists include the Sun, the Moon, stars, clouds, birds, aeroplanes, kites, lightning, a rainbow, a shooting star, and a bright dot that does not twinkle. Add any your child misses, and ask 'have you seen this?'
flow.context: This is the first step of the sky sorting game. You start by listing everything you have seen in the sky.

flow.do: Sort the slips into two piles: 'in our air' and 'out in space'.
flow.say: Now let's sort them. Which of these are close by, in our air? Which are far out in space?
flow.kid: Sort your slips into two piles. In our air. Out in space. Which pile is each one in?

ask.q: Is a cloud in our air or out in space? What about the Moon?
good: Clouds are in our air.
The Moon is out in space.

flow.do: Take the 'out in space' pile and sort it again into three piles. The piles are 'makes its own light', 'does not make its own light' and 'not sure'.
flow.say: Now look at the space pile. Which of these make their own light? Which do not? Put the ones you're unsure about in a separate pile. We'll find out in this unit.
flow.kid: Look at the space pile. Which make their own light? Which do not? Not sure? Put it in a 'not sure' pile.

check.q: Before we test anything, what do you think? Does the Moon make its own light?
check.why: This is a guess before we find out, so any honest answer is a good start. In fact the Moon makes no light. It shines with sunlight bouncing off it. You will test this in the Own Light or Reflected Light experiment.

flow.think: The Sun shines in the day and the stars at night. Are they the same kind of thing, or different?

activities.context: This is a short sorting game. You list everything you have seen in the sky, then sort it into what is in our air, what is in space, and what makes its own light.

activities.title: The Kitchen-Table Sun, Earth and Moon

materials.item: a peppercorn, for the Earth
a grain of salt or a poppy seed, for the Moon
a football, or a round ball about 22 centimetres wide, for the Sun
a ruler, and a measuring tape or a long corridor to pace in

activities.safety: If you go out of the flat to pace out the distance, a grown-up comes along.

schedule.what: Guess the distance to the Sun. Build the Earth and Moon. Then pace out where the Sun goes.

activities.record: Draw the model, with the sizes and distances written on it.

flow.do: 1. Stand facing your child, far apart. 2. Walk towards each other until there is no gap at all, and hug. 3. Then ask your child to guess how far away the Sun is.
flow.say: Let's make the space between us zero. Now there's no space at all between you and me. How much space do you think there is between you and the Sun?
flow.kid: Walk to your grown-up until there is no space between you. Hug! Now guess. How far away is the Sun?
flow.context: This is the first step of the kitchen-table model. You start by guessing how far away the Sun is.

flow.do: 1. Put the peppercorn on the table. It is the Earth. 2. Put the grain of salt 6 centimetres away. It is the Moon. Measure with the ruler.
flow.say: If the Earth were this peppercorn, the Moon would be this grain of salt, 6 centimetres away. Between them is almost nothing at all.
flow.kid: The peppercorn is the Earth. Put the grain of salt 6 centimetres away. That is the Moon. Look how far apart they are!
flow.parent: These are real scale sizes. The Earth is about 2 millimetres, the Moon about half a millimetre, 6 centimetres apart. Light would cross this gap in just over 1 second.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the football. 2. Ask where it should go. 3. Pace out 24 metres from the peppercorn, about 30 big grown-up steps, and put the ball there. A building corridor, the terrace or the building compound is usually long enough.
flow.say: Here is the Sun. It's this big compared to the peppercorn Earth. 109 peppercorns would fit across it. Where do you think it goes? On the table? In the next room?
flow.kid: This ball is the Sun. 109 peppercorns fit across it! Where do you think it goes? Guess. Now walk 30 big steps.

ask.q: Stand next to the peppercorn and look at the ball. Does it look big or small from here?
good: Small, because it's far away.
Small. You could hide it behind your little finger at arm's length.

flow.parent: In this model the Sun is a ball about 22 centimetres wide, 24 metres away. From the peppercorn, the ball looks about as big as the real Sun looks in the sky. At this scale, the nearest other star would be another football about 6,500 kilometres away, about as far as from Delhi to London.

flow.do: Stand by the peppercorn. Talk about how empty space is.
flow.say: Is space crowded or empty? The nearest other star in this model would be as far away as London. That's why stars look like tiny dots.
flow.kid: Look at all the empty space! The next star would be as far as London. That's why stars look so tiny.

check.q: In the model, the peppercorn Earth is 24 metres from the football Sun. Where would the nearest other star be?
options: At the end of the street
About as far away as London is from Delhi
check.why: The nearest other star is about 270,000 times as far as the Sun. 24 metres times 270,000 is about 6,500 kilometres, close to the distance from Delhi to London. Picking 'the end of the street' is a very common guess. Space is far emptier than almost anyone imagines.

flow.think: Space is almost all empty. So why does the night sky look so full of stars?

activities.context: In this activity you build the Sun, the Earth and the Moon at their real sizes and distances, using a peppercorn for the Earth. It shows how big the Sun is, and how empty space is.

activities.title: The Planet Dance

materials.item: open space indoors or outside, and a phone or speaker to play music
a yellow dupatta or cloth for the Sun

activities.safety: Walk, don't run. Clear the space of anything sharp or breakable first.

schedule.what: Dance the Sun, the planets and the Moon. Listen to two pieces from The Planets.

activities.record: Draw your dance: who was the Sun, who were the planets, and who went round whom.

flow.do: 1. One person is the Sun, standing in the middle with the yellow dupatta. 2. The others are planets. 3. Each planet walks in a circle round the Sun. The nearest ones walk small, quick circles. The further ones walk big, slow circles. In a small room, two planets are enough.
flow.say: The Sun is in the middle. Planets near the Sun go round fast, in small circles. Planets far away go round slowly, in big circles.
flow.kid: Someone is the Sun, in the middle. You are a planet. Walk in a circle round the Sun. Near ones go fast. Far ones go slow.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Planet Dance. You act out the Sun and the planets going round it.

flow.do: 1. The Sun holds out an arm towards the nearest planet, to show gravity pulling the planet towards the Sun. 2. Show what happens if a planet stops moving forwards: gravity pulls it in. 3. Show what happens if it walks much too fast: it breaks away.
flow.say: The Sun pulls on every planet. That pull is called gravity. Gravity is the force that pulls things towards each other. The planet keeps moving forwards, and gravity keeps bending its path into a circle. Too slow, and it would fall in. Much too fast, and it would fly away.
flow.kid: The Sun's gravity pulls you towards it. You keep walking forwards. Gravity bends your path round. What happens if you stop?

check.q: What keeps the planets going round the Sun?
options: The Sun's gravity, bending their forward movement into a loop
Nothing. They are stuck to the sky
check.why: Each planet is moving forwards, and the Sun's gravity keeps bending its path round. Together these make an orbit. Picking 'wind in space' is a creative guess. But space has no air, so there is no wind to push.

flow.do: 1. Add a Moon. A small child, or someone carrying a toy, walks round one planet while that planet walks round the Sun.
flow.say: Now the Earth gets a Moon. The Moon goes round the Earth, and the Earth goes round the Sun, carrying the Moon along.
flow.kid: Now add a Moon! The Moon goes round the Earth. The Earth goes round the Sun. Can you do both at once?
flow.think: The Moon goes round the Earth, and the Earth goes round the Sun. Does the Sun go round anything?

flow.do: Play two short pieces from The Planets, orchestra music by Gustav Holst, written between 1914 and 1916. Play 'Mars, the Bringer of War' and then 'Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity'. Dance to each.
flow.say: A composer called Gustav Holst wrote music for the planets, over a hundred years ago. Which one sounds like a giant? He wrote nothing for the Earth. What would the Earth's music sound like?
flow.kid: Dance to the Mars music. Now dance to the Jupiter music. Which sounds like a giant? What would Earth's music be?
flow.parent: Holst's music is about the old Roman gods the planets are named after, not the science. Mars was the Roman god of war. Holst wrote no piece for the Earth, and none for Pluto, which was found in 1930, after he finished.

activities.context: This is a dance where family members act out the Sun, the planets and the Moon. It shows how the Sun's gravity keeps the planets going round it.

setup.art: The Sun child holding out an arm towards a walking planet child, with a dotted curved path showing their orbit.
setup.caption: 2. The Sun's gravity bends each planet's path into a circle.

activities.title: The Moon and the Wanderer: a five-night sky diary

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a torch or a phone light to see your notebook, held low so it does not dazzle you
binoculars, if you have them
a free sky map website such as Stellarium Web, to check which dot is a planet and when the Moon is in your view

activities.safety: Go up on the terrace or out after dark only with a grown-up. Stay away from roof edges and balcony railings. Never point binoculars at the Sun.

schedule.what: At dusk, choose your window or balcony. Draw the skyline, the Moon and any bright dots. Check which dot is a planet.
Same spot, same time. Draw the Moon and the planet again.
Same spot, same time. Draw again. Is more of the Moon lit, or less?
Same spot, same time. Draw again.
Draw one last time. Compare all five drawings. Which moved more, the Moon or the planet?

activities.record: Five drawings, each with the date, the time, the skyline, the Moon and the planet, and the nearby stars.

flow.do: 1. Use the sky map to choose five evenings in a row. On each one, the Moon must be in view from your window or balcony at a fixed time (such as 7:30 pm). 2. Go to that same spot each night, at the same time. 3. Draw the skyline: buildings, the water tank, a tree or a mobile tower. 4. Draw the Moon and the brightest dots near it. 5. Use the sky map to check which bright dot is a planet.
flow.say: We'll come back here at the same time for five nights. Draw the skyline first, so we can see if things move. Which dot shines steadily without twinkling?
flow.kid: Draw the skyline first: buildings, tanks, trees. Then draw the Moon. Then the brightest dots. Which dot does not twinkle?
flow.parent: Check Stellarium Web before you start. Type your city and the date, and it shows where the Moon is at 7:30 pm. As a rough guide: if you face west, start 2 or 3 days after the new Moon. If you face south, start about 6 days after it. If you face east, start about 11 days after it. From a city you will see only the brightest stars, often fewer than ten near the Moon. That is enough. Venus and Jupiter are easy to see even from a city. If no planet is in your view, follow the Moon alone, and draw one or two bright stars or the skyline next to it.
flow.context: This is the first night of the five-night sky diary. You draw the Moon and a bright planet from the same place each evening, to see how they move.

flow.do: On nights 2, 3 and 4, go to the same spot at the same time. Draw the skyline, the Moon, the planet and the nearby stars again.
flow.say: Same place, same time. Has the Moon moved? Has its shape changed? What about the planet?
flow.kid: Same place. Same time. Draw it all again. Has the Moon moved? Is more of it lit?
flow.wait: Come back each evening at the same time, for 3 more nights.

flow.do: On night 5, draw one last time. Then lay all five drawings side by side and compare them.
flow.say: Look at all five nights. Which moved the most, the Moon or the planet? Did the stars keep their pattern?
flow.kid: Put your five drawings in a row. Which moved most? The Moon, or the planet? Did the stars stay still?

check.q: Over five nights, which usually moves a long way against the stars?
check.why: The Moon goes round the Earth in about a month. So at the same time each evening it is a big step further east, about one and a half fists at arm's length. Its lit part also changes shape. Planets move too, but in five nights you may not notice. The stars keep their patterns. Picking 'the stars' usually comes from seeing the whole sky turn during one night. That turning is the Earth spinning, and the stars keep their shapes.

flow.think: If you kept this diary for a whole year, what do you think you would find?

flow.do: Use binoculars on the Moon, held very steady against a wall or railing.
flow.say: Look at the edge between light and dark on the Moon. Those bumps are mountains and craters. Galileo saw them with his first telescope in 1609.
flow.kid: Rest the binoculars on a wall. Look at the Moon. Can you see craters? Galileo saw them over 400 years ago!
flow.parent: Through binoculars, Jupiter may show up to four tiny star-like dots in a line beside it. These are its biggest moons, the ones Galileo found in 1610. Binoculars work well from a city, because the Moon and Jupiter are bright. Only point binoculars at the night sky, never anywhere near the Sun.

activities.context: In this sky diary you draw the Moon and a bright planet at the same time and place for five evenings. You find out that they wander among the fixed stars.

activities.title: The Light Time Machine

materials.item: a kitchen timer or a phone timer
a long strip of paper and coloured pencils, for a timeline

activities.safety: Sit in the sunshine with your eyes closed or looking at the ground. Never look at the Sun.

schedule.what: Feel 8-minute-old sunlight. Make a timeline of when starlight set off.

activities.record: Your timeline of starlight, with a picture at each point.

flow.do: 1. Sit in a patch of sunlight. 2. Set a timer for 8 minutes. 3. While it runs, talk or draw quietly.
flow.say: The sunlight on your arm right now left the Sun about 8 minutes ago. Let's set a timer for 8 minutes. The light that is leaving the Sun now will reach us just as the timer rings.
flow.kid: Sit in the sunshine. Set a timer for 8 minutes. Light leaving the Sun now arrives when it rings!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Light Time Machine. Light takes time to travel, so when we look at the sky we see the past.

flow.do: 1. Draw a long line on the paper strip. Mark 'now' at one end. 2. Mark points for when the light you see tonight set off from the Moon, the Sun, Sirius and the Pole Star. 3. At each point, draw what was happening on Earth.
flow.say: Light from Sirius that you see tonight set off about 8 and a half years ago. Light from the Pole Star set off a few hundred years ago, when there were no cars or electric lights. What was happening in our family when the light from Sirius left?
flow.kid: Make a starlight timeline. Mark when light left the Moon, Sun, Sirius and Pole Star. Draw what was happening then.

ask.q: What was happening in your family when Sirius's light set off, about 8 and a half years ago?
good: I wasn't born yet.
I was a baby.

flow.parent: Astronomers do not agree exactly how far the Pole Star is. Its light set off somewhere between about 300 and 450 years ago. Sirius is the brightest star at night and easy to see from a city, low in the south-east on winter evenings. Light from the Andromeda galaxy set off about 2 and a half million years ago. You can see it with your eyes alone only from a very dark place, never from a city.

flow.do: Talk about what this means when we look at stars.
flow.say: When you look at a star, you see it as it was when its light set off. Some stars you see might have changed since then.
flow.kid: When you see a star, you see its old light. You are looking into the past!

check.q: The light from the Pole Star set off a few hundred years ago. So when you see the Pole Star, you are seeing…
options: The star as it was a few hundred years ago
The star as it is right now
check.why: Light takes time to travel, so we always see a star as it was when its light left. Picking 'as it is right now' is very natural, because light seems to arrive instantly. Over short distances it nearly does. Across space, even light takes years.

flow.think: If someone on a planet 300 light-years away looked at the Earth through a giant telescope tonight, what would they see?

activities.context: This activity uses a timer and a timeline to show that light takes time to travel. When you look at the Sun's light or a star, you are seeing the past.

projects.title: The Shoebox Night Sky

materials.item: a shoebox with a lid
a sheet of black chart paper
a pin and a thicker needle or a sharp pencil point
a torch, or a phone torch
a small bead, a piece of thin wire or a toothpick, and tape
a star map of the Saptarishi and Orion, from a book or a sky app

projects.safety: A grown-up helps with the pin and needle. Poke holes onto a thick pad of old newspaper, never towards your hand.

schedule.what: Copy two star patterns onto black paper. Poke the stars, small holes for faint stars and bigger ones for bright stars. Fit the paper into the box lid.
Add a moving planet bead on a wire. Put the torch in the box and show the family your night sky on the ceiling.

projects.record: Draw the patterns you made and label the stars you know. Write one thing your family asked you.

flow.do: 1. Look at a star map of the Saptarishi and Orion together. 2. Copy the stars onto the black paper with a white pencil. Make bright stars a bigger dot.
flow.say: Let's make our own night sky. Look at the map. Which stars are brightest? We'll make those holes bigger.
flow.kid: Look at the star map. Copy the Saptarishi and Orion onto black paper. Make the bright stars bigger dots.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shoebox Night Sky project. You make a model of two star patterns that you can shine onto a ceiling.

flow.do: 1. Put the black paper on a thick pad of newspaper. 2. Poke a pinhole for each faint star and a needle hole for each bright star. 3. Tape the paper inside the shoebox lid, over a big window cut in the lid by a grown-up.
flow.say: Small holes for faint stars, bigger holes for bright ones. Real stars look faint or bright for two reasons. Some are bigger and hotter, and some are nearer.
flow.kid: Poke a small hole for each faint star. Poke a bigger hole for each bright star. Ask a grown-up to cut the window.
flow.parent: A bright star can be bright because it is very big and hot, like Rigel, or because it is fairly near, like Sirius. From Earth we cannot tell which just by looking.

flow.do: Tonight, with a grown-up, look from a window, the balcony or the terrace for one of your two star patterns. Orion is up on evenings from December to April. The Saptarishi is low in the north on evenings from February to June.
flow.say: Let's see if we can find the real pattern in the sky tonight. Tomorrow we'll add a wanderer to our box and show everyone.
flow.kid: Tonight, with a grown-up, look for Orion or the Saptarishi in the real sky. Tomorrow you will add a planet to your box.
flow.wait: Finish the box the next day.

flow.do: 1. Push a bead onto a thin wire or toothpick. 2. Tape the wire so the bead sits just under the paper, where it can slide along a line between the stars.
flow.say: Planets wander among the stars. Your bead is a planet. Slide it a little each 'night' and the stars stay still.
flow.kid: Put a bead on a wire. Tape it under the paper. Slide it slowly. It is a wandering planet!

flow.do: 1. Put the torch inside the box, pointing up at the lid. 2. Make the room dark. 3. Your child shows the family the star patterns on the ceiling, and slides the planet.
flow.say: Show us your sky. Which stars are suns? Which dot is a wanderer, and where does its light come from?
flow.kid: Switch off the lights. Shine your sky on the ceiling. Show your family the star patterns. Make the planet wander!

check.q: In your shoebox sky, the bead is a planet. In the real sky, where does a planet's light come from?
check.why: A planet makes no light of its own. It shines because sunlight bounces off it. In your shoebox, the bead blocks the torch light, so it shows as a small dark shape. In the real sky, a planet glows because the Sun lights it up. Picking 'the stars around it' is a thoughtful guess. But stars are so far away that their light on a planet is tiny next to the Sun's.

flow.think: In your box, the torch makes every star. In the real sky, what makes each star shine?
flow.parent: The star dots are sharpest when the light comes from one small point, like a phone torch or a small LED. Hold the box close to the ceiling, about 1 to 2 metres away. A wide torch gives blurry dots.

projects.context: In this 2-day project, you poke star patterns into black paper and shine a torch through them onto the ceiling. You add a bead planet that wanders among the stars.

challenges.title: Build a Safe Sun Viewer
challenges.problem: Design and build a viewer that shows a clear, round picture of the Sun at least 2 centimetres wide, so your family can watch a cloud cross it. Nobody may look at the Sun itself.
constraints: Nobody looks at the Sun, or through the viewer at the Sun.
Use only things from home, like boxes, foil, card, paper and tape.
The picture of the Sun must be at least 2 centimetres wide.
materials: a long cardboard box or a tube
aluminium foil, white paper, card and tape
general: A long box with a pinhole in foil at one end and white paper at the other. You look in through a side window, with your back to the Sun.
Two cards. One has a pinhole. Hold it up and catch the Sun's picture on the second card in its shadow.

The picture is about 1 centimetre wide for every metre between the hole and the paper. A shoebox gives a picture only about 3 millimetres wide. For 2 centimetres you need about 2 metres, so the two-card way, with the paper on the floor, is easier than a long box.
creative: Hold a kitchen colander or a straw hat with holes over white paper. Every hole makes its own little Sun.
Look at the shadow under a leafy tree. The round bright spots are all pictures of the Sun, made by gaps between the leaves. During an eclipse they turn into crescents.

Cover a small mirror with paper, leaving one small hole. A grown-up angles it to send the Sun's picture onto a shady wall inside the flat, several metres away. Never look into the mirror, and never point it at anyone.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own viewer. Draw it, build it, and measure your Sun's picture. Can you make it bigger and still sharp?

flow.do: Read the problem together, and the rule that nobody looks at the Sun.
flow.say: Our job is to make a picture of the Sun at least 2 centimetres wide. Remember the pinhole experiment. What made the picture bigger?
flow.kid: Your job: make the Sun's picture 2 centimetres wide. Never look at the Sun! What made the picture bigger last time?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Safe Sun Viewer challenge. You design a viewer that shows a picture of the Sun without anyone looking at the Sun.

flow.do: Before building anything, draw three ideas.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. Let's draw three different ideas.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas before you build any.

flow.do: 1. Build your best idea. 2. Test it outside with your back to the Sun. 3. Measure the picture. 4. Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Test it. How wide is the Sun's picture? What could you change to make it bigger, or sharper?
flow.kid: Build it. Test it with your back to the Sun. Measure the picture. Change one thing. Test again.
flow.parent: The picture's width is about the distance from hole to paper divided by 108. So 1 metre gives about 1 centimetre, and 2 metres gives about 2 centimetres. A sunny balcony or the stairwell can help. Dark spots that stay on the picture and move slowly over days are sunspots, cooler patches on the Sun. Only the very biggest show up in a pinhole picture, and only now and then.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something new?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Astronomers in India watch the Sun with a spacecraft called Aditya-L1, launched in 2023. Why might they study the Sun from space?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a viewer that shows a picture of the Sun at least 2 centimetres wide, without anyone ever looking at the Sun.

challenges.title: Give Us Back the Stars: a dark-sky street lamp
challenges.problem: Bright lights at night hide the stars, and confuse birds, moths and baby turtles. Design a street lamp that lights the road well but sends as little light as possible up into the sky.
constraints: The 'road' on the floor must still be bright enough to read a book on.
The 'sky', the ceiling above the lamp, should be as dark as you can make it.
Use a torch for the bulb, and only paper, card, foil and tape.
materials: card, aluminium foil, paper cups and tape
a stack of books at the edge of a table
a book to read on the floor
general: Point the torch down at the road, not sideways or up.
Put a hood of card over the top of the torch, so no light can escape upwards.
Line the hood with foil, so light that would go up or sideways is reflected down onto the road.
creative: Use a warm orange cover. Many towns now use warmer, dimmer lights, which disturb animals less.
A lamp that switches on only when someone walks past.
Low lights along the edge of the path, instead of one tall bright lamp.

flow.do: 1. In a dark room, stand a stack of books at the edge of a table. 2. Lay the torch on top, pointing out sideways and a little up, like a bare street lamp that shines everywhere. 3. Look at the ceiling, the walls and the floor.

check.q: Why do city people see fewer stars than village people?

check.why: The stars above a city are the same as above a village. City lights brighten the sky, just as the Sun does in the day, so faint stars are lost. Picking 'fewer stars above cities' is a very natural guess. But the stars are just as far away, and just as many.

flow.do: 1. Draw two ideas. 2. Build one from card, cups and foil. 3. Fit it on the torch, or tilt the torch, and score the ceiling again. 4. Check the book can still be read.

flow.parent: The best fix is to tilt the torch so it points down at the floor beside the table, and put a card hood over it, lined with foil. Real street lamps built this way are called full cut-off lamps. The foil reflects the stray light down, so the road can even get brighter.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and creative ideas together. Talk about who needs dark skies.

flow.think: Baby sea turtles hatch at night and crawl towards the brightest light, which used to be the sea. What happens near a bright beach road?

quiz.p: A bicycle reflector glows brightly when a car's headlights shine on it, and is dark otherwise. Which object in the sky is it most like?
opts: The Moon, which shines only when sunlight falls on it
quiz.why: A reflector makes no light. It sends back light that falls on it, just as the Moon and the planets send back sunlight. The Sun and other stars make their own light. Picking 'a star' fits how bright the reflector looks, but not where its light comes from.

quiz.p: Titan, one of Saturn's moons, is bigger than the planet Mercury. So why is Titan called a moon and not a planet?
opts: Titan goes round a planet, Saturn. Mercury goes round the Sun
Moons are always bigger than planets
quiz.why: What makes a moon is what it goes round, not its size. A moon goes round a planet. A planet goes round the Sun. Picking 'made of ice' is a fair guess, but some moons, like ours, are rock.

quiz.p: In the near lamp, far lamp test, the torch looked tiny and dim at 40 steps. What does this tell us about stars?
opts: Stars could be huge suns that look tiny because they are very far away
quiz.why: The torch did not change. Only its distance did. So a tiny-looking star could be a giant sun, very far away. Picking 'stars are tiny' means trusting how big something looks, without asking how far away it is.
quiz.context: In the near lamp, far lamp test, a helper walks away from you with a torch, and you watch how big and bright it looks.

quiz.p: Your friend says, 'The Sun must be the biggest star, because it looks the biggest.' Which test from this unit best shows why this reasoning is not enough?
opts: The near lamp, far lamp test: the same torch looked smaller when it was further away
The Own Light or Reflected Light test
quiz.why: The torch never changed, yet it looked smaller far away. So how big a light looks depends on how far away it is, not only on how big it is. The Sun looks biggest because it is nearest. Many stars are bigger.

quiz.p: Every night for two weeks, you draw a bright dot and the stars around it. The stars keep the same pattern, but the dot slowly moves past them. What is the dot?
quiz.why: Planets go round the Sun much nearer to us than the stars, so night by night they wander past the far-away stars. That is why the Greeks called them wanderers. An aeroplane would cross the sky in minutes, not keep coming back.

quiz.p: Where does a star's twinkle happen?
quiz.why: The twinkle is made in our air, which bends the thin beam of starlight this way and that. Above the air, astronauts see stars shine steadily. Picking 'inside the star' is natural, because that is just what it looks like.

quiz.p: How many planets go round our Sun?
quiz.why: There are eight: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Picking nine comes from the years when Pluto was counted. Picking five comes from the planets you can see without a telescope.

quiz.p: What keeps the Earth going round the Sun?
quiz.why: The Earth is always moving forwards, and the Sun's gravity keeps bending its path into a loop. Picking 'wind' is a creative guess, but space has no air, so there is no wind.
quiz.context: In the Planet Dance, family members walk round a person who is the Sun, as the planets go round the real Sun.

quiz.p: Where in the Sun does fusion, hydrogen joining up to make helium, happen?
opts: Deep in the centre, where it is hottest and most squeezed
All over the surface, like a fire
quiz.why: Atoms only join when they are squeezed very hard and very hot. That happens only in the Sun's centre, at about 15 million degrees. The energy then takes a very long time to work its way out to the surface. Picking 'flames' imagines the Sun as a fire, but there is no burning.

quiz.p: The Sun has been shining for about four and a half billion years. What has been happening to the hydrogen in its centre all that time?
opts: Slowly turning into helium, so there is less hydrogen and more helium
quiz.why: Every second, fusion turns a huge amount of hydrogen into helium. The Sun is so big that it has enough hydrogen for about 5 billion more years. Picking 'smoke' imagines burning, but fusion makes helium, not smoke.

quiz.p: Who found out, in 1925, that stars are mostly hydrogen, even though a famous astronomer said it was impossible?
quiz.why: Cecilia Payne used Meghnad Saha's idea to read the lines in starlight. Picking Galileo is a common guess, because he is famous for the sky. But he lived about 300 years earlier.

quiz.p: Do scientists fully agree on how the Moon was born?
opts: No. Most think a planet crashed into the young Earth, but they still argue about the details
Yes. The Earth caught it as it passed by
quiz.why: The giant crash idea is the favourite, but scientists still argue about exactly how it happened. Picking 'the Earth caught it' is an old idea. Moon rocks are too like Earth rocks for that to fit well.

quiz.p: Where were most of the atoms in your bones and blood made?
quiz.why: Calcium, iron, carbon and oxygen were all made inside stars that died before the Sun was born. Picking 'in your kitchen' is funny and half true. Your food is where your body gets them, but the atoms themselves were made in stars.

opts: Yes. Scientists have found more than 6,000 of them
No. Only the Sun has planets
quiz.why: Since 1992, astronomers have found more than 6,000 planets round other stars. Picking 'nobody can ever know' was a fair answer before then. Now we have the evidence.

quiz.p: In a solar eclipse, the Moon covers most of the Sun. Is it safe to look straight at the Sun then?
opts: No. The small part still showing is bright enough to burn your eyes, and you would not feel it happening
Yes, because most of the Sun is hidden
Yes, if you look for less than a minute
quiz.why: Even a thin edge of the Sun is far too bright for eyes. The back of the eye has no pain sensors, so the harm happens without hurting. Watch an eclipse with a pinhole viewer instead, with your back to the Sun.

applications: Sunlight powers almost all life on Earth. Plants catch it to make food, and animals eat the plants.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, on rooftops, in fields and on spacecraft.
Sailors and travellers have found their way by the stars for thousands of years, using the Pole Star to find north.
Calendars come from the sky. A day is one spin of the Earth, a month comes from the Moon, and a year is one trip round the Sun.
Farmers in many parts of India have long timed sowing and festivals by the Moon and the stars.
Splitting starlight into colours tells astronomers what stars are made of, how hot they are and how fast they move.
India's Aditya-L1 spacecraft, launched in 2023, watches the Sun to understand storms on the Sun that can harm satellites and power lines.
India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023. It studied the soil there, in a region where scientists hope to find ice.
Satellites going round the Earth, lit by the Sun, help with weather forecasts, phone maps and television.
Scientists are building fusion machines that copy the Sun, hoping to make clean electricity one day.
Telescopes in India, such as those at Hanle in Ladakh and Devasthal in Uttarakhand, study stars and exoplanets.
Towns that switch to lamps shining only downwards save electricity and give people back their stars.

open_questions.q: Is there life on any planet round another star?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found more than 6,000 exoplanets, and some might have water. But nobody has yet found a sign of life on any of them.

open_questions.q: Exactly how was the Moon born?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think a planet the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth. But the details, and why Moon rocks are so like Earth rocks, are still argued about.

open_questions.q: What is dark matter, if it exists?
open_questions.why_open: Galaxies spin as if something unseen is holding them together. Machines are trying to catch it, but none has found it yet. Some scientists think gravity itself may work differently.

open_questions.q: Why is the Sun's thin outer layer, its corona, much hotter than its surface?
open_questions.why_open: The surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, but the corona is over a million degrees. Spacecraft like NASA's Parker Solar Probe and India's Aditya-L1 are studying why.

open_questions.q: How many stars have planets like the Earth, at just the right distance for water?
open_questions.why_open: Small, Earth-sized planets are hard to find. Scientists have found some, but they are still counting.

open_questions.q: Will the Sun swallow the Earth when it grows into a red giant, in about 5 billion years?
open_questions.why_open: The Sun will swell up enormously, and will probably swallow Mercury and Venus. Whether it reaches the Earth depends on details scientists still work out.

open_questions.q: How many galaxies are there, and does the universe have an edge?
open_questions.why_open: We can only see as far as light has had time to travel since the universe began. Beyond that, nobody knows how much more there is.

maths.problem: In the near lamp, far lamp test, Meera gave the torch a brightness score at four distances: 2 steps scored 5, 10 steps scored 4, 20 steps scored 2, and 40 steps scored 1. Draw a bar chart of these scores. Then answer: between which two distances did the score drop the most?
maths.answer: Between 10 steps and 20 steps, where the score dropped by 2. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each distance, as tall as its score. Then find each drop. From 2 to 10 steps, the score went from 5 to 4, a drop of 1. From 10 to 20 steps, it went from 4 to 2, a drop of 2. From 20 to 40 steps, it went from 2 to 1, a drop of 1. The biggest drop is 2, between 10 and 20 steps.
maths.context: This is about the near lamp, far lamp test. A helper walks away from you with a torch, and you give it a brightness score from 5 for dazzling to 1 for a faint dot.

answer_chart.title: How bright the torch looked at each distance (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: A list of scores is hard to compare. A bar chart shows at a glance how the light fades as it gets further away.

maths.problem: In the kitchen-table model, the Earth is a peppercorn 2 millimetres wide. The Sun is 109 times as wide as the Earth. About how wide should the model Sun be, in centimetres?
maths.answer: About 22 centimetres, about as wide as a football.
maths.explain: 109 is close to 110. 110 lots of 2 millimetres is 220 millimetres. There are 10 millimetres in 1 centimetre. So 220 millimetres is 22 centimetres. That is about as wide as a football.
maths.context: In the kitchen-table model, you build the Sun, the Earth and the Moon at their real sizes compared with each other, using a peppercorn for the Earth.
maths.why_maths: '109 times as wide' is hard to picture. Multiplying it out with a peppercorn turns a giant number into a ball you can hold.

maths.problem: In the pinhole Sun experiment, the Sun's picture was about 1 centimetre wide when the paper was 1 metre from the hole. How wide would it be at 2 metres? And at 3 metres?
maths.answer: About 2 centimetres at 2 metres, and about 3 centimetres at 3 metres.
maths.explain: Each extra metre adds about 1 more centimetre to the picture's width. So 2 metres gives about 2 centimetres, and 3 metres gives about 3 centimetres. The picture grows in equal steps, a pattern: 1, 2, 3. This works because the Sun is about 108 of its own widths away from us.
maths.context: In the pinhole Sun experiment, sunlight goes through a tiny hole in foil and makes a small round picture of the Sun on white paper.

answer_chart.title: Distance to the paper and width of the Sun's picture

maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you plan a Sun viewer before you build it: to get a bigger picture, you know exactly how much further away the paper must go.

maths.problem: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. Some light leaves the Sun at 4:10 in the afternoon. At what time does it land on your hand?
maths.explain: Start at 4:10 and count on 8 minutes: 4:11, 4:12, and so on up to 4:18. So the light that left the Sun at 4:10 lands on your hand at about 4:18.
maths.context: In the Light Time Machine activity, you sit in the sunshine with an 8-minute timer, because sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us.
maths.why_maths: Light takes time to travel. Counting on minutes on a clock shows exactly how old the sunlight on your hand is.

maths.problem: One evening near the full Moon, the Moon rose at 6:00 in the evening. The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, on average. About what time will it rise tomorrow? And the day after?
maths.answer: About 6:50 tomorrow, and about 7:40 the day after.
maths.explain: Add 50 minutes to 6:00. 6:00 and 50 minutes is 6:50. Then add another 50 minutes. 6:50 and 10 minutes is 7:00, and 40 more minutes makes 7:40. So the Moon rises at about 6:50 tomorrow and about 7:40 the day after. The real time changes a little from day to day, so check it in a sky app.
maths.context: In the five-night sky diary, you watch the Moon at the same time each evening. The Moon rises later each day, because it moves along its path round the Earth.
maths.why_maths: Adding minutes on a clock helps you plan when to go out and find the Moon, and shows that the Moon is really moving round us.
