roots.context: We have been learning that the Sun is a star, that the stars are suns, and that the Moon and planets shine with the Sun's light. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A torch looked dazzling up close, and like a faint star 40 steps away. The Sun and the stars are the same kind of thing. The nearest star after the Sun is about 270,000 times further away. So from a planet of another star, our Sun would look like one more faint star.
deep_truth.habit: We sort the sky into 'the Sun', big and special, and 'the stars', small and far. That split comes from how far away they are, not from what they are.
deep_truth.evidence: The same torch looked dazzling up close and like a faint star at 40 steps. Sunlight and starlight have the same dark lines, made by the same atoms. In 1838 Bessel measured a star so far away that it must shine like a sun.

three.who_am_i: Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star. You are made of what stars make.
three.what_is_life: Almost all life runs on the Sun's light. Plants use sunlight to make their food, and every meal you eat began with a plant catching sunlight.
three.what_is_this_world: The sky is full of suns. In the daytime, the light that shows you the Moon, a leaf and your own hand all comes from one star.

roots.thread: About 4 and a half billion years ago, one cloud of gas and dust pulled itself together. Its middle became the Sun, and what was left round it became the planets, the Earth among them. Older stars had made the atoms in that cloud, and those atoms became rocks, water and you. So the Sun, the Earth and your body began in one cloud, from atoms made by stars that died before. This means we are not outsiders looking at the stars. We are made of what stars made.

teachings.teaching: There, the Sun does not shine, nor the Moon and the stars. When that shines, everything shines after it. By its light, all this is lit.
teachings.link: The Moon shines only with the Sun's light. The Upanishad goes one step further. It says that even the Sun is known only by the light of awareness, the light by which we know anything at all. This is a teaching, not a science finding.

teachings.teaching: A seeker speaks to the Sun: gather your dazzling rays, so I can see your most beautiful form. The person who is there, in the Sun, that am I.
teachings.link: Science finds that the atoms of your body were made in stars. The Upanishad goes further and says that the one in the Sun and the one in you are the same. That is a belief, not a measurement.

teachings.teaching: The cosmos is within us. We are made of star-stuff.
teachings.link: An American astronomer, speaking as a scientist, says what the stars' atoms tell us: we come from them.

science.text: Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star. Margaret Burbidge and her colleagues showed how, in 1957.
The Sun, the Earth and the other planets all formed together from one cloud of gas and dust, about 4 and a half billion years ago.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, and many astronomers today
other_view.view: The Sun is a ball of hot gas, and we are made of atoms, and that is all. Being made of star atoms is chemistry. It does not mean that we and the stars are one being. This is an honest view, held by many thoughtful people.

practice.title: Eight-minute-old sunlight
practice.say: Let's sit in a patch of sunshine by a window or on the balcony. Close your eyes. Never look at the Sun. Feel the warmth on your face and arms. This light left the Sun about 8 minutes ago and travelled 15 crore kilometres before it reached you. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out. Now open your eyes and look at a leaf, or your hand. That same sunlight is reflecting off it into your eyes. Sit quietly for a moment with that.
practice.kid: Sit in the sunshine. Close your eyes. Feel the warm light. It left the Sun 8 minutes ago. Breathe slowly. Open your eyes. Look at your hand.

ask: Is the Sun 'ours', or is it just the star we happen to live near?
If someone on a far-off planet saw our Sun as a tiny star, would they be wrong?
When moonlight falls on your face, whose light is it?
When you see a bright star, can you tell if it is big and far, or smaller and nearer? How could you find out?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged in sunshine with eyes closed, a thin golden thread of light running from the Sun to the child, and from the child up to a sky full of tiny suns.

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, most people believed the stars were small lights fixed to a great ball round the Earth, not far beyond the planets. Some Greek thinkers reasoned like this. If the Earth really went round the Sun, a nearby star should seem to shift a little over a year, as the Earth moved from one side of its path to the other. Nobody could see any shift, so most people decided the Earth must stand still. The real reason was that the stars are far too distant for the shift to be seen by eye. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel, a German astronomer, used a very fine telescope to watch a faint star called 61 Cygni for over a year. It shifted by a tiny amount, about as much as a coin seen from 15 kilometres away. From that shift he worked out that its light takes about 10 years to reach us. A star that far away can only be seen at all if it shines like a sun. So the stars are suns.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The stars are small lights fixed close beyond the planets, and since no star seemed to shift, the Earth must stand still. Bessel measured a star's tiny yearly shift and showed it is so far away that it must be a sun.
